متقدّم آخر تحقّق: 2026-09-21. تستشهد هذه الصفحة بحقائق تتغيّر مع الوقت — اعتبر التاريخ أعلاه دليلًا على حداثتها. تأكّد من المصدر الرسمي. What you'll learn Place AX correctly in Google's stack: Kubernetes, Agent Sandbox, Agent Substrate, AX, then your harness Read the four AX resources (Task, Workspace, Gateway, Model) and know what each one buys you Explain what really survives an AX suspend/resume, what does not, and what your runner image must do about it Run a first Task end to end with ax apply, ax watch and ax ssh, and know the three debugging traps Decide when a self-hosted runtime like AX beats Claude Managed Agents or the OpenAI Agents API, and when it does not On the night of September 20, 2026, AX: Google's open agentic orchestrator went to the top of Hacker News with 507 points and 222 comments. Most of those comments were people asking what it is for. That is a fair question, because the project has been public since May 20, 2026 (v0.1.0) and has changed shape twice since, so most of the blog posts you will find describe a CLI that no longer exists. Here is the short version. AX is not a model, not an agent framework and not a hosted service. It is a Kubernetes-style control plane, with a kubectl-shaped CLI, that takes a declared agent Task, gives it a sandbox, clones its repos, wires its MCP servers and skills, fences its network, and can freeze it to a snapshot and thaw it later on any free worker. It sits under whatever harness you already use, whether that is Claude Code, Google's ADK, LangChain, or a Python loop you wrote yourself.
documents.s: AX (Agent Executor): Google's Open Agent Runtime, Explained for Builders (2026)

documents.t: The Google announcements use four names that are easy to confuse. They are four layers, and AX is the top one. Layer What it is Status (Sep 2026) Numbers Google publishes Kubernetes / GKE The cluster — — Agent Sandbox (kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox) A Sandbox CRD: gVisor-isolated pods (Kata pluggable), warm pools, pod snapshots GA on GKE since May 21, 2026 300 sandbox allocations/s per cluster; sub-second start, 90% within 200 ms Agent Substrate (agent-substrate/substrate) A minimal control plane that multiplexes many idle actors onto few warm workers by snapshotting RAM + files to object storage Open source, early, "not an officially supported Google product"; managed flavour on GKE in evaluation ~250 stateful actors on 8 pods; "10x higher density" than plain containers; sub-second activation AX (google/ax) Declarative Tasks/Workspaces/Gateways/Models + CLI on top of Substrate v0.3.0, ax.io/v1alpha1, Apache-2.0, 4.3k stars "billions of tasks per cluster" (marketing claim, not a benchmark) Your harness Claude Code, ADK, LangChain, A2A agents, your own loop — — Two things the table hides. First, Substrate is where the interesting engineering lives (the snapshot and teleport machinery); AX is the ergonomic layer. Second, Substrate lives in its own GitHub org, not under google/, which several HN commenters flagged as a signal about how official any of this is. Treat the whole thing as a serious but pre-1.0 open-source project from a Google team, not a product with an SLA.
Everything in AX is a YAML resource in an atespace (Substrate's tenancy unit; default unless you say otherwise). You ax apply -f them exactly as you would with kubectl.

apiVersion: ax.io/v1alpha1 kind: Task metadata: name: fix-flaky-test spec: image: "ghcr.io/my-org/my-agent-image" command: ["my-agent", "--goal", "fix the flaky test"] env: - name: ENVIRONMENT value: "staging" resources: requests: { cpu: "500m", memory: "1Gi" } limits: { cpu: "2", memory: "4Gi" } workspaces: - name: golang path: "/workspace" goal: "Ensure the Go toolchain is available and built from source" gateway: name: default-gateway debug: true A Task is deliberately small. The concepts doc describes agents creating many Tasks over their lifetime rather than living inside one long process. Three fields matter more than they look: workspaces[].goal is a plain-English description of the environment the Task needs. AX's "generative" setup tries to complete the workspace from that sentence (install a toolchain, fetch dependencies). It is the one place where a model is in the loop before your agent starts. debug: true is the only way to get ax ssh into the sandbox. Without it the guest services are not exposed and the CLI refuses to connect. gateway is optional in the schema, but if you leave it out you are relying on whatever the substrate's default egress policy is. Declare one.
documents.s: Task: the unit of isolated execution

documents.t: apiVersion: ax.io/v1alpha1 kind: Workspace metadata: name: golang spec: git: - name: origin repo: "https://github.com/golang/go.git" branch: "my-fix" mcp: registries: - provider: google query: "mcp.tags:build" servers: - name: git-tools endpoint: "http://git-mcp.default.svc.cluster.local:8080" skills: registries: - provider: google query: "skills.tags:nodejs" path: "/.agents/skills" This is the resource that makes AX more than "Kubernetes Jobs with a sandbox". A Workspace pre-clones repositories, resolves MCP servers (by explicit endpoint or by a registry query), and drops skill packages into a path. Note the default skills path: /.agents/skills is the same directory convention the cross-agent SKILL.md standard uses for Codex, Cursor and Gemini CLI, so a Workspace can hand the same skills to whichever harness runs inside the Task.
documents.s: Workspace: git + MCP + skills, materialised before the agent starts

documents.t: apiVersion: ax.io/v1alpha1 kind: Gateway metadata: name: default-gateway spec: listeners: - name: http port: 8080 protocol: HTTP egress: allowlist: hosts: - host: "api.anthropic.com" port: 443 The reference manifest ships with host: "*" on 443, which is an allow-everything policy. Change it. Egress allowlists are the single most effective control against the exfiltration patterns in our prompt-injection and what your agent uploads pages, and AX gives you a declarative place to put them. Listeners are how a Task exposes a port (for an A2A endpoint, a dev server, a debug UI); ax tunnel forwards them to your laptop.

apiVersion: ax.io/v1alpha1 kind: Model metadata: name: claude-model spec: provider: anthropic model: claude-opus-5 secretKey: name: anthropic-api-secret key: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY parameters: maxTokens: 16000 temperature: 0.9 The reference docs show google and anthropic providers. The credential is a reference to a Kubernetes Secret, so the manifest never contains the key and the key is rotated where you already rotate secrets. AX is not Gemini-only; the runner docs do mention that GEMINI_API_KEY is injected automatically when the atespace has Gemini credentials, which is the one place Google's own model gets a shortcut.
documents.s: Model: provider + model ID + a Kubernetes secret

documents.t: This is the part no launch post covers, and it is where you will lose an afternoon if you skip it. From docs/runner.md: The entrypoint is fixed. Whatever spec.image you supply, the controller starts the container with /usr/local/bin/ax-task-runner as PID 1. Your image must contain an executable at that path (a symlink is fine). The published base image is gcr.io/ax-substrate/ate-images/ax-task-runner, and extending it is the normal route. Your command arrives via environment, not argv. The runner receives AX_TASK_YAML (the whole Task, including status) and AX_WORKSPACES_YAML (every bound Workspace as multi-document YAML), parses spec.command out of the Task, and starts it as a child process with the first workspace as the working directory. It also exposes AX_METADATA_URL, a small local HTTP metadata server. Bootstrap has a 10-minute clock. Workspace materialisation (clones, MCP resolution, skill install, the generative goal step) must finish within AX_BOOTSTRAP_TIMEOUT, default 10 minutes. Large monorepos on a cold worker can blow through it. The control plane does not read your exit code. The runner logs the command's exit status but stays up as PID 1 whether or not your agent is still running. So a Task in phase Running does not mean your agent is alive. Write your own completion signal (a file in the workspace, a message to your own queue, a Task deletion from inside) and watch that. Shutdown is SIGTERM, 10 seconds, SIGKILL. The runner forwards SIGTERM to the command's process group and waits a bounded grace period. Flush state early.
documents.s: What actually happens inside a Task

documents.t: Suspend/resume is the feature that justifies the whole stack. Agents spend most of their wall-clock waiting on a model, a tool, or a human, and Substrate's bet is that an idle agent should cost storage, not a warm pod. ax suspend task fix-flaky-test # Ready=False, snapshot taken ax resume task fix-flaky-test # restored on any free worker What the docs say survives, and what does not: Survives a suspend/resume Does not survive The /workspace volume (files, clones, build artefacts) The process tree: your agent restarts from its entrypoint Substrate-level actor memory snapshot (RAM + files, at the Substrate layer) Open network connections (GKE docs: agents must handle reconnection) Task spec and status Anything written outside the workspace volume The runner doc is explicit about the consequence: after resume, the runner sees the same files but a new process tree, so it must track whether workspace setup already ran (marker files are the suggested mechanism) or it will re-clone every repo. If your agent keeps its plan or its conversation only in process memory, a resume loses it; keep the transcript on disk in the workspace. This is the same lesson as our long-running agent harnesses page, enforced by the infrastructure. Guided walkthrough1 of 6 1Install the CLI and point it at a cluster⌄ go install github.com/google/ax/cmd/ax@latest. AX follows your active kubeconfig context (kubectx works) and defaults to namespace ax-system and atespace default. For a laptop, the Agent Substrate repo's hack/ scripts stand up a kind cluster with the substrate installed; AX's control plane is then deployed with make deploy AX_IMAGE_REPO=<your registry>, which needs ko and a registry you can push to. ←PreviousNext→ 2Build a runner image⌄ FROM the published ax-task-runner image, apt-get or npm install your agent, keep /usr/local/bin/ax-task-runner as the entrypoint. Do not override ENTRYPOINT; put the agent in spec.command instead. ←PreviousNext→ 3Write the four manifests⌄ One Model with a secretKey pointing at an existing Kubernetes Secret, one Gateway with a real egress allowlist (your model provider, your git host, nothing else), one Workspace with the repo and any MCP servers, one Task with debug: true for the first run. ←PreviousNext→ 4Apply and watch⌄ ax apply -f manifests/ then ax watch task <name>. Wait for the WorkspaceReady and GatewayReady conditions before Ready. If Ready never comes and the phase flips to Failed, the 10-minute bootstrap timeout is the first suspect. ←PreviousNext→ 5Get inside⌄ ax ssh <name> -- ls -al /workspace shows what the Workspace actually materialised; ax ssh <name> -- env | grep AX_ shows the runner contract. Both only work because you set debug: true. ←PreviousNext→ 6Suspend, resume, and check your own completion signal⌄ ax suspend task <name>, wait, ax resume task <name>, then confirm your agent picked up from disk rather than restarting the job. Finally ax delete task <name>: the phase goes to Terminating while the sandbox is torn down. ←PreviousNext→ Have Claude draft the manifests for an agent you already run CopyOpen in Claude↗ I run an agent as a container image ghcr.io/acme/triage-agent:1.4. Its entrypoint is "triage --repo REPO_PATH --model MODEL_ID". It needs: the repo github.com/acme/backend on branch main, an MCP server for Linear reachable at http://linear-mcp.tools.svc.cluster.local:8080, outbound access only to api.anthropic.com:443 and github.com:443, and the Anthropic key from the Kubernetes Secret "anthropic-api-secret" (key ANTHROPIC_API_KEY). Write the four google/ax v1alpha1 manifests (Model, Gateway, Workspace, Task) for this, following docs/manifests.md in the repo. Then write a Dockerfile that extends the published ax-task-runner base image and installs my agent WITHOUT changing the entrypoint. Finally, list what I must change in the agent so that (a) it treats the first workspace as its working directory, (b) it survives a suspend/resume by keeping its plan and transcript on disk under /workspace and using a marker file to skip re-setup, and (c) it signals completion in a way the AX control plane can't (it ignores exit codes).

The most-upvoted question in the HN thread was "what is the benefit over the OpenAI Agents API?" The honest answer is that they are different layers. AX + Agent Substrate Claude Managed Agents OpenAI Agents API Cloudflare's isolate runtime Who runs the loop You (any harness in the container) Anthropic (the harness is theirs) OpenAI (the Codex harness) You, on Workers/Durable Objects Where it runs Your Kubernetes cluster, any cloud or on-prem Anthropic's infrastructure OpenAI's, or a self-hosted sandbox Cloudflare's edge Isolation gVisor / Cloud Hypervisor sandbox per Task Anthropic-managed environment Hosted or self-hosted sandbox V8 isolate, container on demand Model choice Any provider you put in a Model resource Claude OpenAI models Any (via API) Idle cost model Snapshot to storage, resume on demand Session-based billing Session-based billing Isolates hibernate You own Cluster, upgrades, secrets, egress policy An API key An API key A Workers account Pick AX when you need data sovereignty, want to run more than one vendor's model behind one policy, already operate Kubernetes, or want agents that can sleep for days without paying for compute. Pick a hosted loop when you want a working harness today and do not want to own a cluster. Many teams will do both: a hosted loop for interactive sessions, AX-style infrastructure for fleets of background Tasks.
documents.s: Where AX sits next to the hosted agent loops

documents.t: The June-era docs describe a different tool. The May preview exposed a conversation-centric CLI (ax exec --conversation … --resume, ax fork for trajectory branching, an AgentService protocol with ADK and A2A bridges). The September README's command reference is resource-centric: apply, get, describe, watch, suspend, resume, delete, ssh, tunnel, ctx. If a tutorial shows ax fork, it is from before the redesign. The five headline capabilities from the May blog (durable execution, isolation, single-writer session consistency, connection recovery, trajectory branching) are still the stated goals; how much of the branching story survives in the resource model is not documented as of this writing. v1alpha1 means it. The README warns of major breaking changes before a stable release. Pin the CLI version and the runner image digest, and re-read docs/manifests.md on every upgrade. Kubernetes is not optional. The most-repeated complaint in the thread. The Substrate quickstart runs on kind, so you can try it on a laptop, but production means a real cluster. If you do not already run Kubernetes, AX is not the reason to start. Managed GKE Agent Substrate has hard requirements. GKE 1.37+ (1.36 with beta flags), Workload Identity, beta APIs enabled at cluster creation, uniform machine types per ActorTemplate (no E2), a Cloud Storage bucket for snapshots, gVisor or Cloud Hypervisor isolation, and no GPU passthrough. Production use is behind an allowlisted private GA program. Egress defaults are permissive in the examples. host: "*" on 443 lets an agent reach any HTTPS endpoint. That is the opposite of what you want for a Task that reads untrusted repos. Follow the same rules as securing local and hybrid agents. Two projects, two orgs, one disclaimer. AX is under google/; Substrate is under agent-substrate/ and states it is not an officially supported Google product. Neither is eligible for Google's OSS vulnerability rewards program. Budget for reading source when something breaks. AX vocabulary اقلبالمصطلحTaskالتعريفThe smallest unit of isolated execution in AX: an image, a command, resources, bound Workspaces and a Gateway. Agents create many Tasks; a Task is not a long-lived agent process.اضغط Enter أو مفتاح المسافة لقلب البطاقة. استخدم مفتاحي السهمين الأيسر والأيمن للتنقل بين البطاقات.تم إظهار المصطلح. ←السابق 1 / 8 التالي→ Check yourself 0/6 1You supply spec.image with your own ENTRYPOINT. What does AX run as PID 1? Your ENTRYPOINT/usr/local/bin/ax-task-runner, alwaysspec.command directlyA shell that sources spec.env 2Your agent exits with status 1. What does ax get task show? FailedSucceededStill Running: the control plane does not read the command's exit statusTerminating 3After ax resume, your agent re-clones every repository. Why? The workspace volume was lostThe Gateway blocked the cacheThe process tree is new, so the runner ran setup again; it should have checked a marker fileResume always re-materialises Workspaces 4ax ssh refuses to connect to your Task. Most likely cause? Wrong kube contextspec.debug is not true, so guest services are not exposedThe Gateway has no listenerYou forgot -a default 5Which layer actually implements snapshotting idle agents to storage and restoring them on a warm worker? AX itselfAgent SubstratekubectlThe Model resource 6A tutorial from June 2026 tells you to run ax fork to branch a trajectory. What should you expect? متوسط On 6 August 2026 OpenAI shipped a mid-cycle refresh of GPT-5.6 that most coverage collapsed into one sentence: "Sol got smarter, free users got unlimited chats." The real update is more interesting — and more consequential if you are a Claude user who occasionally reaches for the OpenAI stack. Three moving parts changed at once: an effort control now runs both in the ChatGPT UI (as a slider) and the API (as a six-tier parameter); a free-tier Think button ships the following week with unlimited Luna chats; and the long-context pricing cliff at 272K input tokens interacts awkwardly with Fast mode, which only runs on Sol. Each shifts a real decision. This page pulls those decisions out of the release-notes fog and shows what actually changes for a builder who thinks in Claude terms. What you'll learn See exactly what shipped on 6 August 2026 for GPT-5.6 — and what shipped the week of 10 August for free users Understand the six-tier effort parameter (`none, low, medium, high, xhigh, max`) and map it onto Claude's thinking-effort model Learn the 272K input-token pricing cliff — and how it can silently double a job you thought you had budgeted Know when Fast mode helps, when it does nothing, and which requests it silently refuses Decide when the update is a real reason to switch a workload from Claude to Sol — and when it's not
documents.s: GPT-5.6 August 2026 Update: Effort Slider, Free Think Button & the 272K Price Cliff

documents.t: Three concrete things. The rest is polish. Guided walkthrough1 of 3 1Effort control, both in ChatGPT and the API⌄ Plus and Pro users see a new slider on web, mobile and desktop that sets how much reasoning ChatGPT uses per response. Under the hood, the API exposes the same knob as `reasoning.effort` with six positions — `none`, `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, `max` — defaulting to `medium` when omitted. This replaces the previous 'model decides' behavior: you now pick the tier and pay for it. ←PreviousNext→ 2GPT-5.6 Sol behavioral pass⌄ OpenAI updated Sol to give 'more direct responses, use tighter formatting, and avoid extra detail when it does not help', to adapt detail per question, and to be 'less likely to agree when a correction would be more helpful' — the closest OpenAI has come to shipping an explicit anti-sycophancy pass. Internal evals on financial, medical and legal prompts reported factual errors were '68% less common' than the retired GPT-5.5 Instant. ←PreviousNext→ 3Free-tier upgrade the week of 10 August⌄ Free users get unlimited text chats on GPT-5.6 Luna (previously capped) and a new Think button for deeper reasoning on harder questions, 'subject to abuse protections'. The Think button was not live on 6 August — it rolled out the following week. ←PreviousNext→ آخر تحقّق: 2026-08-11. تستشهد هذه الصفحة بحقائق تتغيّر مع الوقت — اعتبر التاريخ أعلاه دليلًا على حداثتها. تأكّد من المصدر الرسمي.

If you have been thinking in terms of Claude's five-level effort setting (introduced with Opus 5 in July), the mental model is similar but the labels don't line up cleanly. GPT-5.6 has six tiers where Claude has five, and the semantics differ at both ends. GPT-5.6 tier What it does Roughly like Claude Opus 5 none Skips reasoning entirely; instant answer No direct equivalent — Claude always plans a little low Short chain-of-thought, cheap minimal effort medium (default) Balanced planning; the shipped default low–medium high Deeper planning; slower, dearer medium xhigh Long deliberation; multi-step reasoning high max Full reasoning ceiling — expensive maximum Two practical consequences: The default moved. On the API, if you omit reasoning.effort, you get medium. Previously many wrappers relied on the model auto-selecting effort; that behavior is gone. Explicit is now required for predictable cost. none is a real button. It is genuinely useful for classifier prompts, structured extraction, or tool-router calls where reasoning tokens are pure overhead. Claude has no cleanly-equivalent 'off' switch. A safe request template that pins effort explicitly CopyOpen in Claude↗ { "model": "gpt-5.6-sol", "reasoning": { "effort": "low" }, "messages": [ { "role": "system", "content": "Extract only. Output JSON." }, { "role": "user", "content": "..." } ] }
documents.s: The effort slider — mapping the six tiers to a Claude mental model

documents.t: This is the change most likely to burn a bill unexpectedly. The rule: if a request's input crosses 272,000 tokens, the entire request is re-priced at 2× the input rate and 1.5× the output rate, not just the tokens above the line. There is no proration. Two things about that rule matter: It's a cliff, not a slope. A prompt at 271,999 input tokens pays the base rate. A prompt at 272,001 pays 2×/1.5× on every input and output token in the call — including the reasoning tokens the model generates. Long conversations creep across it. Multi-turn chats and agent loops accumulate history. A session that starts under 272K can silently cross the line on turn 12 and re-price every subsequent turn. Guided walkthrough1 of 3 1Do the arithmetic before you commit⌄ GPT-5.6 Sol base pricing is $5 / $30 per million (input / output), with cached input at $0.50. Above 272K input tokens, the same call costs $10 / $45. On a 300K-token document with 4K output, base cost is $1.62. Cross the cliff and it becomes $3.18 — nearly 2× for one extra token past the threshold. ←PreviousNext→ 2Chunk instead of stuffing when you're near the line⌄ Two 200K calls cost $2 in input. One 400K call costs $8 (2× input on the whole request). Chunking is 4× cheaper for input if either chunk stays below 272K. Only stuff when you truly need the model to see everything at once. ←PreviousNext→ 3Watch cache behavior around the cliff⌄ Cached input at $0.50 is still cached at $0.50 up to 272K. Above the cliff, the multiplier applies to every priced token — including uncached input above the cached prefix. A stable 250K cached prefix plus a growing tail can silently push you over. ←PreviousNext→
documents.s: The 272K token pricing cliff — a real hazard

documents.t: Fast mode is a Sol-only option that trades price for latency: up to 2.5× faster at 2× the API price. Terra and Luna don't offer it. Three things the launch pitch downplays: 'Up to' is a ceiling, not a norm. Wall-clock speedup depends on your workload — tool calls, network hops and streaming rate all cap the realized gain well below 2.5×. Fast mode and long context don't cleanly mix. OpenAI hasn't published a mutual-exclusivity rule, but early guides report Fast mode requests behave badly (or silently degrade) once you cross the 272K input threshold. Treat them as incompatible until OpenAI documents otherwise. Reasoning tokens still count. Fast mode makes throughput faster, but a max-effort call still generates the same volume of reasoning output. The economics only work when you're paying for latency you can actually feel. Pro tip Fast mode's break-even is roughly 25% more throughput per dollar at the 2.5× ceiling — worse when the ceiling isn't hit. Prefer Fast mode for interactive chat where the user waits. Skip it for batch, background agents and long-context RAG. If you were going to switch a batch pipeline from Claude to Sol for cost, don't turn on Fast mode — you'll erase the saving.
documents.s: Fast mode — small print worth reading

documents.t: For a Claude user this matters less than the API changes, but it's the change most likely to show up in a friend's screenshot and start an argument. Unlimited text chats on GPT-5.6 Luna for free ChatGPT users, from the week of 10 August 2026. Previously capped. Think button on free chats, same window. Adds a deeper-reasoning pass to a specific message, subject to abuse protections. It is not the same UI as the Plus/Pro effort slider — it's a per-message toggle, not a session-wide setting. The practical read: OpenAI is aggressively defending the free tier now that Claude and Gemini both have generous free reasoning options. Expect the abuse-protection cap to be tight for the first few weeks.
documents.s: Free tier: unlimited Luna + the Think button

documents.t: For most Claude workloads the answer stays the same. For three specific patterns it moves. Guided walkthrough1 of 3 1You are paying for a lot of no-reasoning classifier calls⌄ `reasoning.effort: none` on Sol Luna is now a plausibly cheaper option than a min-effort Claude Haiku call for high-volume routing, tag extraction, or structured labelling — provided your prompts stay well below 272K. Benchmark it on a representative sample before switching. ←PreviousNext→ 2You have a latency-sensitive interactive workflow⌄ Sol + Fast mode is now the fastest quality tier OpenAI ships. If a user is waiting on each response and your prompts fit under 272K, this is the update that most changes the tradeoff. For background agent runs, ignore it. ←PreviousNext→ 3You do long-context RAG or repo-scale reasoning⌄ The 272K cliff means you should design for it. Claude Opus 5's 1M context and Sol's 1.05M context both extend well past 272K, but Claude does not have a cliff of the same shape — its long-context pricing is flat. For repo-wide operations at 400K+ input, Claude currently has the cost advantage. ←PreviousNext→
documents.s: Where this update actually changes a Claude user's decision

documents.t: If you shipped against Sol before 6 August, two things need to change: Set reasoning.effort explicitly on every call. Omitting it now costs you medium; you probably wanted low for most. Add a 272K guard at the boundary of your pipeline. Reject or chunk requests whose input tokens push past the threshold. A dumb check of len(input) / 4 as an approximation is enough as a first line of defence. A guardrail one-liner for Node.js wrappers CopyOpen in Claude↗ if (estimateTokens(input) > 260_000) { chunkOrReject(input); }

documents.t: Two rumors that were circulating around this update are not part of it: GPT-6 (Astra). As of 11 August 2026 OpenAI had not confirmed a launch date, model card, or pricing. It has since shipped: GA on September 4, 2026 at $10 / $50 per MTok with the same 272K pricing cliff described on this page. See the GPT-6 Astra field guide. Sol pricing drop. The base $5 / $30 rate has not changed. Some coverage confused the 272K cliff (a surcharge) with a price change.

Check yourself 0/4 1You send a 300,000-token input prompt to GPT-5.6 Sol at base pricing. Roughly, what happens to the cost compared to sending 271,000 tokens? Only the tokens above 272K are priced higher; the first 272K stay at base rateThe entire request is re-priced at 2× input and 1.5× output ratesThe request is rejected because Sol's ceiling is 272KNothing changes — 272K is only relevant to Fast mode 2On the API, you omit `reasoning.effort` on a GPT-5.6 Sol call after the 6 August update. What effort tier do you get? `low` — OpenAI defaults to the cheapest tier`medium` — the shipped defaultThe model auto-selects effort based on the prompt`none` — no reasoning until you opt in 3Which of these workloads benefits most from Fast mode? A nightly batch RAG job over a 400K-token knowledge baseA background research agent that runs for an hourAn interactive chat where the user is waiting on each reply, prompts under 272KA high-volume structured-extraction classifier 4Which behavior change did OpenAI ship for GPT-5.6 Sol on 6 August 2026? A hard token limit reduction from 1.05M to 272KA guarantee that Sol always outperforms Claude Fable 5 on coding benchmarks'More direct responses, tighter formatting, less likely to agree when a correction would be more helpful'Removal of tool-use support to reduce hallucinated function calls

متوسط You already think in Claude. Then on 9 July 2026 the whole timeline flipped: OpenAI shipped three GPT-5.6 variants — Sol, Terra, Luna — and ChatGPT Work, an agent that takes a goal and works on it in the background for hours. A teammate asks "should we swap to Sol?"; a client wants ChatGPT Work to replace half a workflow you already run in Claude. This page maps the launch onto your Claude mental model and — more usefully — pulls out the parts the news coverage buries: the real prices, the exact benchmark deltas, the 1.05M context nobody expected, and where OpenAI still loses to Anthropic. What you'll learn Learn what actually shipped: Sol, Terra, Luna (plus Sol Ultra), all with a 1.05M-token context window Read the benchmark table the way OpenAI didn't publish it — where GPT-5.6 leads and where Claude Fable 5 still wins Understand ChatGPT Work: not a chat mode, but a background agent that returns a finished spreadsheet, deck, doc, or web app hours later Know when to reach for GPT-5.6 Sol over Claude for coding, agents, browser tasks — and when the answer is still Claude
documents.s: GPT-5.6 & ChatGPT Work for Claude Users

documents.t: GPT-5.6 is a three-tier refresh of the GPT-5 family — Sol (flagship), Terra (mid), Luna (budget) — sharing a 1.05M-token context window, 128K max output, and an OpenAI-published claim of 54% better token efficiency on agentic coding; ChatGPT Work is the new autonomous agent built on top of it, delivered as a merged desktop app that swallowed Codex. The interesting part isn't the model refresh — that was expected. It's the shape of the release: OpenAI is now shipping model + agent + IDE as one product, and pricing the workhorse tier ($1 in / $6 out on Luna) below where "cheap coding models" have historically sat.
Everyone's writing the benchmark recap. Here are the parts most Claude users miss on the first read.
documents.s: Three things about the GPT-5.6 launch that surprise people

documents.t: This is not how OpenAI usually ships. In earlier refreshes, the cheap tier came with a shrunken context window as a way to nudge you upward. In GPT-5.6, Sol, Terra, and Luna all quote a 1.05M-token context and 128K max output — the same shape. That means Luna at $1 input / $6 output per million tokens is a viable long-context option, not just a short-request one, and it changes the maths for RAG pipelines, whole-repo review, and long tool loops. If you were budgeting a Claude Haiku-style tier for high-volume retrieval work, Luna is now the obvious cross-check.
documents.s: 1. All three tiers share the same 1.05M context

documents.t: The framing OpenAI uses is telling: you don't chat with ChatGPT Work, you brief it. It takes an outcome ("build a competitive analysis of these five vendors"), gathers context from your connected apps and files, breaks the job into steps, works independently for minutes or hours, and delivers a finished artifact — a spreadsheet, slide deck, document, report, or working web app. Codex was folded into the same desktop app, so ChatGPT Work also owns the code-writing surface. This is the same "long-running autonomous work" bet Anthropic made with Claude's managed agents, but shipped as an end-user product first and an API second. It rolled out on Pro / Enterprise / Edu on launch day, with Plus and Business following within days.
documents.s: 2. ChatGPT Work is not "a chat mode" — it's a background agent that hands you a finished file

documents.t: Read past the marketing chart and the picture is more mixed than "Sol is the new king". OpenAI's own numbers say Sol reaches 80 on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index (about +2.8 vs Claude Fable 5) while using less than half the output tokens at roughly a third the cost. That's a real win. But Fable 5 still leads SWE-Bench Pro by a large reported margin — Sol comes in at ~64.6% there — and the launch coverage tends to bury that. Translation: pick by workload, not by press release. For "agent index" style tool-and-browser work, Sol is now the model to beat. For real-repo bug fixes with meaningful context, Anthropic still has the edge.
documents.s: 3. Sol wins the OpenAI-published benchmarks. Claude still leads SWE-bench Pro.

Model Input $/1M Output $/1M Context Max output Positioning Sol $5 $30 1.05M 128K Flagship: complex reasoning, coding, science, agents Terra $2.50 $15 1.05M 128K "GPT-5.5 performance at ~half the cost" — routine work Luna $1 $6 1.05M 128K High-volume, simpler tasks; long-context on a budget Sol Ultra (not disclosed) (not disclosed) 1.05M 128K Higher-effort Sol tier used in some published benchmarks; also the surface that exposes the multi-agent Responses beta Benchmarks OpenAI published (Sol / Terra / Luna): Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index v1.1: 80 / 77.4 / 74.6 SWE-Bench Pro: 64.6% / 63.4% / 62.7% (Claude Fable 5 still leads this one) Terminal-Bench 2.1: 88.8% (Sol Ultra 91.9%) / 87.4% / 84.7% DeepSWE v1.1: 72.7% / 69.6% / 67.2% BrowseComp: 90.4% (Sol Ultra 92.2%) / 87.5% / 83.3% ExploitBench: 73.5% / 52.9% / 33.2% That last row — ExploitBench — is worth staring at. The Sol → Luna drop from 73.5% to 33.2% is much sharper than any other benchmark on the list, which is why OpenAI leaned on the cybersecurity story for Sol specifically and why federal reviewers held the model for extra testing before letting it out.

Given a goal, it works in the background for minutes-to-hours and returns a finished file.اضغط Enter أو مفتاح المسافة لقلب البطاقة. استخدم مفتاحي السهمين الأيسر والأيمن للتنقل بين البطاقات.تم إظهار المصطلح. ←السابق 1 / 6 التالي→

Your prompting instincts still work. Clear instructions, explicit output shapes, few-shot examples, and giving the model tools with good descriptions — all of it moves across, because these are properties of instruction-tuned frontier models, not Claude-specific tricks. For the deep version of that argument see porting prompts across models and the practical guide ChatGPT for Claude users. Two things to reset when you jump: API shape. Anthropic uses a tools block on the messages API; OpenAI uses tools on Chat Completions (or the Responses API), with the OpenAI function-calling schema. Same idea, different wire format. Reasoning as a mode, not just a slider. Claude exposes a thinking/effort parameter; on GPT-5.6, the sharpest gains show up when you pick the right tier (Sol / Sol Ultra) rather than only tuning effort on the cheap one. Cost matters more than it did on GPT-5.5.

documents.t: The OpenAI SDK unchanged — just point model at a GPT-5.6 variant: Call GPT-5.6 Sol from Python (OpenAI SDK) CopyOpen in Claude↗ from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI() # uses OPENAI_API_KEY resp = client.chat.completions.create( model="gpt-5.6-sol", # try gpt-5.6-terra / gpt-5.6-luna to trade cost for quality messages=[ {"role": "system", "content": "You are a careful research agent. Use tools; verify before you conclude."}, {"role": "user", "content": "Compare our 3 largest competitors on pricing, packaging, and 2026 launches."}, ], # tools=[...] # OpenAI-style function/tool schema ) print(resp.choices[0].message.content) Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1Pick the tier before you write the prompt⌄ Sol for complex coding, agent loops, or anything where you'd have reached for a Claude Opus tier. Terra as the default 'GPT-5.5 at half the cost' workhorse. Luna for retrieval, extraction, classification, and other high-volume jobs — the shared 1.05M context makes it a real option, not a toy. ←PreviousNext→ 2Use ChatGPT Work for outcomes, not questions⌄ If the request has a definable artifact at the end (spreadsheet, deck, report, small web app), brief ChatGPT Work and let it run. If it's a conversation or a decision aid, stay in a normal chat. ←PreviousNext→ 3Wire the tools the same way you would for Claude⌄ Describe each tool as if it were a good product spec: clear name, one-line purpose, parameter descriptions with examples. GPT-5.6 responds to the same 'give tools like you'd give a junior' discipline as Claude does. ←PreviousNext→ 4Budget for output tokens, not just input⌄ The Sol/Terra/Luna prices are 6× more expensive on output than input. The 54% efficiency claim is exactly about *output* — verify it on your workload before you migrate a Claude budget over. ←PreviousNext→
documents.s: Try it in a few lines

documents.t: Neither is strictly better. Reach for GPT-5.6 when: You need a $1/$6 tier with a 1.05M context. Luna is currently the cheapest way to get long-context frontier-adjacent quality; that's a new capability, not a rebrand. The task is browser-heavy or agent-index-shaped. BrowseComp and the Coding Agent Index are Sol's strongest cards. If your agent spends most of its time in a browser or a shell, Sol is the model to beat. You want ChatGPT Work's "brief and forget" workflow for producing finished spreadsheets/decks/reports/apps as end-user artifacts, without gluing an agent framework yourself. Reach for Claude when you want the managed platform around the model — prompt caching, memory and context editing, managed agents, computer use, the desktop app — and specifically when the workload is real-repo software engineering, where Fable 5 still leads SWE-Bench Pro by a large margin. See Claude, GPT, Gemini for coding for the ongoing head-to-head, and what AI costs across providers for the cost view. Check yourself 0/3 1Which GPT-5.6 tier has the smallest context window? مبتدئ أنت تفكّر بالفعل بلغة Claude. ثم يُقسِم زميلٌ بأن Grok هو الأفضل للأسئلة عمّا يحدث الآن، أو يحتاج مشروعٌ إلى مساعد موصول مباشرةً بـ X/تويتر، أو يسلّمك أحدهم قاعدة كود على شكل OpenAI ويطلب منك توجيهها إلى xAI بدلًا من ذلك. الخبر السار: كل ما تعرفه تقريبًا ينتقل معك — وفي جانب واحد (الـ API) يكاد التبديل يكون مجّانيًا. هذه الصفحة تُسقِط نموذجك الذهني الخاص بـ Claude على Grok من xAI، وتُشير إلى الحفنة القليلة من الأشياء التي تعمل فعلًا بشكل مختلف، وتخبرك متى يميل Grok إلى أن يكون الخيار الأفضل. What you'll learn ترجمة مفاهيم Claude إلى مكافئاتها في Grok (تطبيق Grok، وواجهة xAI API + الكونسول، ومتغيّرات النموذج، وGrok Build) معرفة أيٌّ من عاداتك في صياغة الأوامر مع Claude ينتقل دون تغيير (جميعها تقريبًا) فهم الميزتين المميّزتين الحقيقيتين لـ Grok: البحث الفوري الأصيل في X/الويب، وواجهة API متوافقة مع OpenAI معرفة متى يميل Grok إلى التألّق — العمل الحيّ/على الأحداث الجارية، وعمليات الهجرة السلسة من OpenAI آخر تحقّق: 2026-07-01. أسماء النماذج الدقيقة، وأرقام الإصدارات، وأحجام نافذة السياق، ومستويات الخطط، والأسعار تتغيّر باستمرار في xAI (فقد أطلق Grok عدّة إصدارات فرعية في 2026 وحده). تُعلّمك هذه الصفحة النموذج الذهني الدائم وربط المفاهيم؛ ولأي اسم أو حدّ أو سعر محدّد، راجع وثائق xAI الحالية نفسها (المرتبطة في المصادر) بدلًا من الوثوق برقم هنا. تأكّد من المصدر الرسمي.

إن قرأت قسمًا واحدًا فقط، فاقرأ هذا. إليك كيف تصطفّ الأشياء التي تعرفها في Claude مع عالم Grok: في Claude تسمّيه… في عالم Grok هو… الفكرة نفسها؟ Claude.ai (تطبيق المحادثة) تطبيق Grok (grok.com، وتطبيقات X، والموبايل) نعم — الواجهة الاستهلاكية/المساعِدة مُنتقي النموذج (Opus / Sonnet / Haiku) متغيّرات Grok (نموذج رائد مثل Grok 4.3، ومتغيّر سريع لاستدعاء الأدوات، ومتغيّر برمجي) نعم — الفكرة نفسها، بأسماء مختلفة Claude Code (البرمجة الوكيلة في الطرفية) Grok Build (واجهة سطر أوامر لوكيل البرمجة من xAI) قريب — انظر أدناه الكونسول / API + مساحة العمل واجهة xAI API (https://api.x.ai/v1) + كونسول xAI نعم — واجهة المطوّر للنمذجة والحصول على مفتاح استخدام الأدوات / استدعاء الدوال (API) Function calling (بشكل متوافق مع OpenAI) نعم — الحلقة نفسها، وهنا حتى الـ JSON مألوف البحث في الويب / الاستشهادات بحث فوري أصيل في X + الويب مدمَج في النموذج قريب — لكن أكثر "حيويةً" بوضوح الخلاصة: لا يكاد يوجد مفهوم جديد لتتعلّمه. الأمر في معظمه إعادة تسمية وإعادة تموضع لأشياء تفهمها بالفعل — زائد مجالين يتجاوز فيهما Grok حدود Claude فعلًا: الوصول الفوري إلى بيانات X/الويب، وواجهة API متوافقة مع OpenAI جاهزة للاستبدال المباشر.

هذا هو الفرق الذي يغيّر أكثر ما يغيّر للمطوّرين: واجهة xAI API تتّبع مواصفة واجهة OpenAI. عنوان الأساس هو https://api.x.ai/v1، فإن كان لديك كود يتحدّث بالفعل مع عميل متوافق مع OpenAI، فالهجرة غالبًا مجرّد تغيير عنوان الأساس واستبدال المفتاح. آخر تحقّق: 2026-07-01. توثّق xAI واجهتها بأنها متوافقة مع OpenAI بعنوان أساس https://api.x.ai/v1؛ لكن السطح المتوافق الدقيق (أيّ المعاملات ونقاط النهاية تتطابق بنظافة) يتطوّر — تحقّق من دليل البدء السريع الحالي لدى xAI. تأكّد من المصدر الرسمي. بالنسبة لمستخدم Claude يستحق هذا أن يُستوعب، لأن واجهة Messages في Claude لها شكلها الخاص (صيغة طلب/ردّ خاصة، وكتل tool_use/tool_result خاصة). قادمًا من Claude، عدّل ردّة فعلك هكذا: Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1وجّه إلى OpenAI SDK، لا إلى Anthropic⌄ يُوصَل إلى Grok عبر عملاء على طراز OpenAI. لا تترجم إلى لهجة ثالثة — بل تُعيد استخدام شكل طلب OpenAI الذي تعرفه أنت (أو مكتبة) بالفعل. ←PreviousNext→ 2غيّر عنوان الأساس + المفتاح⌄ اضبط عنوان الأساس على https://api.x.ai/v1 واستخدم مفتاح xAI. يظلّ الكثير من بنيتك التحتية المتوافقة مع OpenAI يعمل. ←PreviousNext→ 3أعِد استخدام JSON استدعاء الأدوات حرفيًّا تقريبًا⌄ لأن الصيغة متوافقة مع OpenAI، تنتقل تعريفات استدعاء الدوال بشكل مباشر أكثر بكثير ممّا تنتقل بين Claude وOpenAI — راحة حقيقية، لا فخّ. ←PreviousNext→ 4تأكّد مع ذلك من معرّف النموذج⌄ الشيء الوحيد الذي عليك ضبطه بدقّة هو اسم النموذج (مثلًا معرّف grok-4.x حالي). معرّفات النماذج هي أسرع التفاصيل تغيّرًا — راجع صفحة النماذج الحيّة. ←PreviousNext→ هجرة بالاستبدال المباشر (Python، بـ OpenAI SDK) CopyOpen in Claude↗ from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI( api_key="YOUR_XAI_KEY", # an xAI key, not an OpenAI key base_url="https://api.x.ai/v1", # the only structural change ) resp = client.chat.completions.create( model="grok-4.3", # confirm the current id in xAI docs messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize today's top AI headline."}], ) print(resp.choices[0].message.content) Watch out الاستبدال المباشر ≠ سلوك متطابق. صيغة السلك متوافقة مع OpenAI، لكن النموذج هو Grok — تختلف شخصيته، وحدود رفضه، ومعرفته الفورية. أعِد تشغيل تقييماتك؛ لا تفترض أن موجّهًا مضبوطًا لـ Claude (أو GPT) يؤدّي الأداء نفسه. لا تلصق أبدًا مفتاح API حيًّا في موجّه، أو مستودع، أو محادثة. استخدم متغيّرات البيئة وإدارة الأسرار، تمامًا كما تفعل مع مفتاح Anthropic.
documents.s: الـ API جاهز للاستبدال المباشر — وهذه هي النقطة الكبرى للبنّائين

documents.t: هنا يفترق Grok أكثر ما يفترق عن عاداتك في Claude. بُني Grok بواسطة xAI بـ وصول فوري أصيل إلى المعلومات من X (تويتر) والويب، وتضع xAI البحث الحيّ كجزء أساسي من طريقة إجابة النموذج. آخر تحقّق: 2026-07-01. تصف xAI نموذج Grok باستخدام أدوات أصيل وتكامل بحث فوري (بما في ذلك بيانات من X)؛ لكن سلوك الاسترجاع الدقيق، ومدى الحداثة، وأيّ حدود بحسب الخطة تتغيّر — تحقّق من صفحات منتَج xAI الحالية. تأكّد من المصدر الرسمي. بالنسبة لمستخدم Claude، التحوّل الذهني هو هذا: مع Claude تلجأ إلى أداة بحث، أو خطّ استرجاع، أو موصِّل حين تحتاج معلومات حالية، وتفكّر بعناية في حدود معرفتك الزمنية. مع Grok، "ما الذي يحدث الآن على X / على الويب" أقرب إلى إعداد افتراضي مدمَج. وهذا يجعل Grok خيارًا طبيعيًا للأسئلة الحيّة، وعن الأحداث الجارية، ونبض الشبكات الاجتماعية — ويغيّر ما ينبغي أن تشكّك فيه: النتائج الحيّة ما زالت تحتاج انضباط التحقّق من المصادر نفسه الذي تطبّقه على أي محتوى ويب. Pro tip اعتمد على Grok على محور الحداثة: الأخبار العاجلة، والنقاشات الرائجة، و'ماذا يقول الناس اليوم'. هذا هو موطن قوّته بنيويًّا. احتفظ بغرائز Claude في التحقّق: الفوري ≠ الموثوق. اطلب المصادر، وعامِل المنشور الفيروسي كادّعاء يُتحقّق منه، لا كحقيقة. للحداثة عمر نصف. للمواد المرجعية الدائمة، قد تتقادم إجابة البحث الحيّ أو تُفرِط في الاتّكاء على أعلى الأصوات الأخيرة — انظر الملاحظة أدناه. للفكرة الأعمق عن لماذا الحداثة والحقيقة ليستا الشيء نفسه، انظر الحداثة وعمر النصف والهلوسة — كلاهما ينطبق مباشرةً على أي مساعد يعتمد البحث الفوري.
documents.s: البحث الفوري في X + الويب هو العنوان الحقيقي

documents.t: إن كنت تعيش في Claude Code، فإن Grok Build من xAI هو أقرب مكافئ: وكيل برمجة تقوده من الطرفية، ينافس في المضمار نفسه الذي فيه Claude Code وCodex CLI من OpenAI. بُني حول متغيّر Grok مضبوط للبرمجة ونهج وكلاء فرعيين متوازيين للعمل عبر قواعد كود أكبر، مع وضع مستقلّ طويل الأمد لتسليم المهام الأكبر. آخر تحقّق: 2026-07-01. أطلقت xAI واجهة سطر أوامر لوكيل البرمجة (Grok Build) ومتغيّر نموذج مضبوط للبرمجة؛ لكن التوفّر (مثلًا أيّ مستوى اشتراك)، ومجموعة الميزات الدقيقة، ومعرّف النموذج تتحرّك بسرعة — عامِل التفاصيل على أنها حسّاسة زمنيًّا وتحقّق منها. تأكّد من المصدر الرسمي. تنتقل المفاهيم واحدًا لواحد تقريبًا من Claude Code: فكرة Claude Code مكافئ Grok Build ملاحظات تعديلات وكيلة من الطرفية نفسها — وكيل برمجة بواجهة سطر أوامر الحلقة الجوهرية (قراءة ← تخطيط ← تعديل ← تشغيل) هي الشكل المشترك لهذه الفئة بأكملها وكلاء فرعيون / عمل متوازٍ بنية وكلاء فرعيين متوازيين كلاهما يقسّم العمل الكبير عبر مساعِدين؛ تختلف تفاصيل التنسيق مهامّ مستقلّة طويلة الأمد وضع "أنجِز الهدف" طويل الأمد سلّم تنفيذًا أكبر ودَعه يخطّط-ينفّذ-يتحقّق النقطة الدائمة: مهارة قيادة واجهة سطر أوامر برمجية وكيلة قابلة للنقل. كتابة مهمة واضحة، وإبقاء السياق محكمًا، ومراجعة الفروقات، والتوجيه بنقاط تفتيش — كلّها الانضباطات نفسها سواء كان الوكيل هو Claude Code أو Codex أو Grok Build. انظر ما هو Claude Code؟ للنموذج الذهني، ووكلاء البرمجة المحلّيون للمجال الأوسع.
documents.s: Grok Build هو جواب xAI على Claude Code

documents.t: معظم درايتك بـ Claude تنتقل. إليك القائمة القصيرة للأشياء المختلفة فعلًا: لهجة الـ API (في صالحك). يتحدّث Grok بشكل متوافق مع OpenAI، لا بـ Anthropic Messages. إن كنت قادمًا من واجهة Claude، فأنت تنتقل إلى شكل طلب/ردّ OpenAI — وتكسب إعادة استخدام سهلة لأي شيء مبنيّ سلفًا لنقاط النهاية المتوافقة مع OpenAI. الفوري بشكل افتراضي. التأريض على الأحداث الجارية أقرب إلى أن يكون مدمَجًا في Grok. عدّل متى تلجأ إليه — واستمرّ في التحقّق من المصادر. الشخصية والحدود. نبرة Grok وحدوده على المحتوى مضبوطة بشكل مختلف عن Claude. لا تفترض أن موجّه نظام معايَرًا لأسلوب Claude يُنتج النبرة نفسها أو الرفض نفسه. التفاصيل المتقلّبة. أسماء النماذج، والمتغيّرات، وحدود السياق، والأسعار تتحرّك بسرعة (أطلق Grok إصدارات متعدّدة عبر 2026). اكتسب عادة التأكيد من المصدر — تمامًا كما ينبغي أن تفعل مع Claude أيضًا.
documents.s: ما الذي يحتاج فعلًا إلى تعديل

documents.t: كلاهما مساعد عام قادر، والفارق في أي مهمة بعينها كثيرًا ما يكون صغيرًا ومتبدّلًا — فعامِل هذا على أنه ميول، لا قوانين، ودَع تقييمك على بياناتك يقرّر: العمل الحيّ وعلى الأحداث الجارية. "ما الذي يحدث الآن"، والمواضيع الرائجة، وأسئلة نبض الشبكات الاجتماعية تلعب لصالح بحث Grok الفوري الأصيل في X/الويب. الهجرات السلسة من OpenAI. إن كان لديك كود متوافق مع OpenAI، فتوجيهه إلى xAI من أقلّ عمليات التبديل احتكاكًا في المجال. تسليمات البرمجة أوّلًا-في-الطرفية. إن كنت تحبّ سير عمل Claude Code / Codex، فإن Grok Build خيار ثالث طبيعي لتجرّبه اختبارًا مقارنًا على مهامّك. الجواب الصادق في معظم الأحيان: أيّهما أنت (أو فريقك) مُعَدّ فيه بالفعل، وأيّهما يفوز في تقييمك على المهمة التي تهم. المهارة قابلة للنقل؛ تكلفة الإعداد هي تكلفة التبديل الحقيقية. للطريقة المحايدة تجاه المزوّد في الاختيار، انظر اختيار نموذج وما تكلفة الذكاء الاصطناعي عبر المزوّدين. مفردات من Grok إلى Claude اقلبالمصطلحتطبيق Grok (grok.com / داخل X)التعريفالواجهة الاستهلاكية/المساعِدة لـ xAI، مرتبطة بإحكام بـ X. ≈ Claude.ai.اضغط Enter أو مفتاح المسافة لقلب البطاقة. استخدم مفتاحي السهمين الأيسر والأيمن للتنقل بين البطاقات.تم إظهار المصطلح. ←السابق 1 / 6 التالي→ اختبر نفسك 0/3 1لديك خدمة مكتوبة بالفعل مقابل عميل متوافق مع OpenAI وتريد تجربة Grok. ما الخطوة الدائمة الأقلّ احتكاكًا؟ أعِد كتابة كل شيء إلى صيغة واجهة Messages في Claude أولًاغيّر عنوان الأساس إلى https://api.x.ai/v1، واستبدل بمفتاح xAI، واضبط معرّف نموذج Grok حاليلا تستطيع — لدى xAI لهجة API مملوكة بالكامل 2مهمة هي 'لخّص ما يقوله الناس عن إعلان اليوم على X.' لماذا قد يكون Grok الخيار الطبيعي — وأيّ انضباط ما زال ينطبق؟ Grok دائمًا أدقّ من Claude، فلا حاجة لأي تحقّقبحث Grok الفوري الأصيل في X/الويب يناسب الأسئلة الحيّة/الحالية، لكن عليك مع ذلك التحقّق من المصادر ومعاملة المنشورات الفيروسية كادّعاءاتClaude وحده يستطيع الوصول إلى الويب، فهذا سؤال خادع 3أنت تحبّ سير عمل Claude Code. ما الطريقة الدقيقة للتفكير في Grok Build؟ نموذج مختلف تمامًا عليك إعادة تعلّمه من الصفرالفئة نفسها من واجهات سطر أوامر البرمجة الوكيلة — مهارات القيادة تنتقل، تختلف فقط تفاصيل التنسيق والنموذجأداة بواجهة رسومية فقط بلا سير عمل طرفي Key takeaways لا يكاد يوجد مفهوم جديد: تطبيق Grok ≈ Claude.ai، ومتغيّرات Grok ≈ Opus/Sonnet/Haiku، وGrok Build ≈ Claude Code، وfunction calling ≈ استخدام الأدوات. الـ API هو الفرق البارز — فهو متوافق مع OpenAI (عنوان الأساس api.x.ai/v1)، فالكود على شكل OpenAI يُهاجَر باستبدال عنوان الأساس + المفتاح، بخلاف واجهة Messages الخاصة بـ Claude. البحث الفوري في X/الويب أقرب إلى أن يكون مدمَجًا في Grok — الجأ إليه للحداثة والأحداث الجارية، لكن احتفظ بانضباط Claude في التحقّق من المصادر. Grok Build وكيل برمجة طرفي في مضمار Claude Code / Codex؛ ومهارة قيادة واجهة سطر أوامر وكيلة قابلة للنقل. الأسماء والمتغيّرات وحدود السياق والأسعار تتقادم بسرعة في xAI — تحقّق من التفاصيل في وثائق xAI، تمامًا كما ينبغي مع Claude.

متوسط On 15 July 2026, Thinking Machines Lab — Mira Murati's lab — released Inkling, its first in-house model, as open weights under Apache 2.0. It hit the front page of Hacker News overnight, and the coverage settled into two lazy shapes: "trillion-parameter open model!" and a benchmark table showing it losing. Both miss the point. Inkling is an unusual release that is deliberately not trying to top the leaderboard, and its most interesting feature — a continuous thinking-effort dial trained into the weights — has been widely mis-described in the first wave of reporting. This page is the practical read. What you'll learn Understand what Inkling actually is: a 975B sparse MoE with 41B active, Apache 2.0, 1M context, natively multimodal across text/image/audio/video Learn what the thinking-effort dial really is — a continuous float trained via RL, not the discrete low/medium/high enum the API wrappers show you See why 'open weights' does not mean 'runs on your machine' — the real VRAM floor is ~600 GB even quantized Know why Inkling loses benchmarks on purpose, and the one metric where it wins that nobody put in a headline

Inkling is a Mixture-of-Experts transformer with 975B total parameters and 41B active per token, pretrained on 45 trillion tokens of text, images, audio and video, supporting a 1M-token context window, released under Apache 2.0 — positioned not as the best model available, but as the best base to customize. That last clause is the whole strategy. Thinking Machines says so plainly: Inkling "is not the strongest overall model available today, open or closed." Shipping a model alongside that sentence is not modesty, it's positioning — and it explains every design decision below.

This is the headline feature and it's the most mis-reported detail of the launch. Several outlets described the effort parameter as ranging "0.2 to 0.99," or as a named enum — none | minimal | low | medium | high | xhigh. The official Tinker documentation says something different. Effort is continuous reasoning-effort conditioning: any float from 0.0 inclusive up to, but not including, 1.0. The default is 0.9. The named levels are just recommended sweep values, not the actual interface: Preset Value none 0.0 minimal 0.1 low 0.2 medium 0.7 high 0.9 xhigh 0.99 The 0.2 floor that got reported is simply the low preset — not a limit. Nothing stops you passing 0.45. Note also how non-linear the presets are: the gap from low to medium is 0.5, while high to xhigh is 0.09. The useful resolution is bunched up at the top of the range. This matters because most people will meet Inkling through an OpenAI-compatible wrapper exposing reasoning_effort="high". That enum is a lossy adapter over a continuous knob. If you're tuning cost against quality, the enum hides most of the dial. Set effort directly via the Tinker renderer CopyOpen in Claude↗ renderer = TmlV0Renderer(get_tokenizer("thinkingmachines/Inkling")) messages = [Message(role="user", content="Solve this problem step by step.")] prompt = renderer.build_generation_prompt(messages, effort=0.9) The same effort argument carries into fine-tuning, which is the part worth pausing on — you can train at a chosen effort level: Fine-tune at a fixed effort level CopyOpen in Claude↗ model_input, weights = renderer.build_supervised_example( messages_with_assistant_response, effort=0.9, ) آخر تحقّق: 2026-07-16. تستشهد هذه الصفحة بحقائق تتغيّر مع الوقت — اعتبر التاريخ أعلاه دليلًا على حداثتها. تأكّد من المصدر الرسمي.
documents.s: 1. The effort dial is a float, and the news got its range wrong

documents.t: The reason the dial is continuous is that it wasn't bolted on at inference time. During reinforcement learning, the team set effort by changing the system message and adjusting the per-token cost — literally taxing the model for thinking. The model learned to spend different token budgets on different rollouts, and the dial is the residue of that training. That's a genuinely different mechanism from "please think step by step, but briefly," and it's why the payoff is real: Thinking Machines reports Inkling matches Nemotron 3 Ultra on Terminal Bench 2.1 while using roughly one-third as many reasoning tokens. It also explains the caveat the docs are careful to state, which you should take seriously: "Larger values generally encourage more reasoning, but do not guarantee longer responses or higher accuracy on every sample." Effort is a learned tendency, not a guarantee. Turning it to 0.99 and expecting monotonic improvement is a misread of what it is. And higher effort "may require a larger generation budget to avoid truncation" — crank effort without raising max tokens and you'll cut the model off mid-thought.
documents.s: 2. Effort isn't a prompt trick — it was trained in with a token tax

documents.t: "975B parameters, Apache 2.0, weights on Hugging Face" invites an assumption the hardware table demolishes: Numeric Aggregated VRAM floor Example configuration BF16 at least 2 TB 8× NVIDIA B300, or 16× NVIDIA H200 NVFP4 (W4A4) at least 600 GB 4× NVIDIA B300 NVFP4 (W4A16) at least 600 GB 8× NVIDIA H200 Even fully quantized to 4-bit, the floor is roughly 600 GB of aggregated VRAM. This is a multi-GPU-cluster model, not a workstation model, and not remotely a laptop model. The 41B active parameters make it cheap to run a token through; they do nothing to reduce what you must hold in memory. All 975B parameters have to be resident, because the router may reach for any of them on any token. If your interest in open weights is "run it locally," Inkling is the wrong model and running models locally with Ollama is the right page. If your interest is legal freedom to modify and commercialize — Apache 2.0, genuinely permissive — then Inkling qualifies, and you'll rent the GPUs from TogetherAI, Fireworks, Modal, Databricks or Baseten. Those are different reasons to want open weights, and this release serves only the second one.
documents.s: 3. Open weights, but you almost certainly can't run it

documents.t: The benchmark table is unflattering, and Thinking Machines published it anyway: Benchmark Inkling A stronger competitor Terminal Bench 2.1 63.8% GLM 5.2: 82.7% SWEBench Verified 77.6% Kimi K2.6: 80.2% SimpleQA Verified 43.9% DeepSeek V4 Pro: 57.0% FORTRESS Adversarial 78.0% Nemotron 3 Ultra: 77.6% Three losses, one narrow win. But the interesting result isn't in that table at all — it's calibration. The team trained with reinforcement learning based on proper scoring rules, which reward a model for saying "I'm 70% sure" and being right 70% of the time, rather than for sounding confident. The model was rewarded for estimating its own uncertainty well instead of confidently producing wrong answers, and it shows up on forecasting evaluations like ForecastBench and Prophet Arena. For anything where a wrong-but-confident answer costs more than a hedged one — triage, research, routing, extraction with a human reviewer downstream — a well-calibrated 44% is worth more than an overconfident 57%. That property doesn't fit in a leaderboard column, which is roughly why nobody led with it.
documents.s: 4. It loses benchmarks on purpose — and wins the one nobody reported

documents.t: The pieces worth knowing, beyond the parameter count: Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Sparse MoE routing⌄ A 66-layer decoder-only transformer. Each layer holds 256 routed experts plus 2 shared experts, with 6 routed experts active per token. The shared experts always fire — they carry general capability — while the router picks specialists per token. ←PreviousNext→ 2Relative positional embeddings, not RoPE⌄ A deliberate departure from the near-universal default. The stated reason is better extrapolation to longer sequences, which is how a 1M-token context window is meant to hold up rather than degrade at the tail. ←PreviousNext→ 3Attention shape⌄ Sliding-window and global layers mixed at a 5:1 ratio with 8 KV heads, plus short convolutions applied at the attention inputs. Five cheap local layers per one expensive global layer is what makes 1M context affordable. ←PreviousNext→ 4Native multimodality⌄ Images enter as 40×40 pixel patches through a four-layer hMLP; audio as dMel spectrograms. Both pass through a lightweight embedding layer and are processed jointly with text tokens — one stream, not a bolted-on vision encoder. Output is UTF-8 text only. ←PreviousNext→ 5Hybrid optimizer⌄ Muon for large matrix weights, Adam for everything else — an unusual choice at this scale, and consistent with the lab's public research interest in optimizer behavior. ←PreviousNext→

Reach for Inkling when: You need to own and modify a capable multimodal model. Apache 2.0 plus real multimodality plus first-class fine-tuning support on Tinker is a rare combination. This is the intended use. Cost per task matters more than peak score. The effort dial at one-third the reasoning tokens is a real lever, and you can tune it continuously rather than in three steps. Calibration matters. If your pipeline can act on "the model isn't sure," this is unusually well-suited. Don't reach for it when you want the strongest coding agent (the table says GLM 5.2 and Kimi K2.6 beat it), when you want to self-host on your own hardware (see the VRAM floor), or when you want maximum factual recall (SimpleQA 43.9% is not competitive). One safety note that the model card states directly: Inkling has a residual "occasional tendency to comply with role-play and indirectly framed prompts concerning harmful topics," and the card explicitly recommends layering external moderation — it names Llama Guard — rather than relying on built-in refusals. VentureBeat framed the model's posture as "resistance to censorship"; read the model card's own language as the operative guidance instead, and budget for a moderation layer if you deploy this. The card also lists the usual residual limits: hallucination, imperfect instruction-following, and degraded performance in long multi-turn conversations. Check yourself 0/4 1What is the actual valid range of Inkling's thinking-effort parameter? A float from 0.0 inclusive up to, but not including, 1.0A float from 0.2 to 0.99One of six named levels: none, minimal, low, medium, high, xhighAn integer from 1 to 10 2Inkling has 41B active parameters out of 975B total. What does that mean for memory? You only need enough VRAM for ~41B parametersAll 975B parameters must be resident in memory; the sparsity cuts compute, not memoryThe inactive experts stream from disk on demand at no costMemory scales with context length only 3Why did Thinking Machines train Inkling with proper scoring rules in RL? To make responses shorterTo top the SWEBench leaderboardTo improve calibration — so stated confidence tracks actual accuracyTo enable multimodal input 4Setting effort=0.99 instead of 0.9 guarantees what? A longer responseHigher accuracy on every sampleNothing guaranteed — it encourages more reasoning but the docs warn it may need a bigger generation budget to avoid truncationLower latency

If you already read Kimi K2 for Claude users, the shape is familiar — a trillion-ish-parameter sparse MoE with permissive licensing — but the intent differs. Kimi K2 optimizes for long agentic tool chains. Inkling optimizes for being reshaped: multimodal input, a tunable effort budget, and fine-tuning as a first-class path. For the broader picture, see choosing a model, DeepSeek and Qwen open models for the rest of the open-weights field, and what AI costs across providers for the economics the effort dial is aimed at. آخر تحقّق: 2026-07-16. تستشهد هذه الصفحة بحقائق تتغيّر مع الوقت — اعتبر التاريخ أعلاه دليلًا على حداثتها. تأكّد من المصدر الرسمي.

متقدّم On 14–16 July 2026, xAI published Grok Build — the coding agent behind its CLI — as a public Apache 2.0 repository at xai-org/grok-build. Not the weights. The harness: the agent loop, the tool implementations, the terminal UI, the extension system. It went to the front page of Hacker News within hours. This is a rare artifact. Almost every serious coding agent — Claude Code, Cursor, Codex — ships as a binary or a bundle. Here, roughly 800,000 lines of production Rust are sitting in a repo you can read. That's worth more as a textbook than as a product. This page is the practical read: what's actually in there, what the structure teaches you about building agents, and two things about this release that most of the coverage got backwards. What you'll learn Understand what was published and what wasn't — harness yes, weights no, development history no Read the crate map as a checklist of what a production coding agent actually needs Learn why Apache 2.0 here means source-available, not open-development — and why that distinction is load-bearing See the data-collector code still present in the published tree, and what its constants confirm about the July exfil incident Know what's genuinely reusable from this repo and what is a dead end
documents.s: Inside Grok Build: Reading an Open Agent Harness

documents.t: The repository is 99%+ Rust, licensed Apache 2.0, and describes itself as a coding agent harness and TUI — fullscreen, mouse-interactive, extensible. It builds on macOS and Linux with a pinned Rust toolchain. Three things it is not: Not the model. Grok 4.5's weights are not here and are not open. The harness talks to a hosted endpoint. You can read every line of how the agent thinks about your codebase and still not run it without xAI's API. Not a development history. The repo has two commits: Publish harness and TUI open-source, then Synced from monorepo. There's a SOURCE_REV file at the root containing a single internal revision hash. This is an export of a private monorepo, re-synced periodically — not a repository that was developed in public and not one you can archaeologize for design decisions. Not open to you. CONTRIBUTING.md states plainly that the repository does not accept external pull requests or unsolicited patches, that xAI develops the software internally, and that the tree is published "for source transparency and local builds." GitHub issues are disabled at the repo level. ★ The distinction that matters: Apache 2.0 is a license, and it grants you real rights — read, fork, modify, ship derivatives. It says nothing about governance. Grok Build is source-available under an open-source license with a closed development model. You may fork it; you may not influence it. Read "open source" in the headlines as "you can read the source," because that is exactly and only what is on offer.

Ignore the marketing. The directory listing under crates/codegen/ is the most useful thing in the repo, because it is an honest inventory of what a shipping coding agent needs. A selection: Crate What it tells you xai-grok-agent, xai-grok-shell The agent runtime and its entry points — interactive, stdio, headless xai-grok-tools, xai-grok-tools-api Tool implementations, split from the tool interface — a real boundary xai-grok-workspace, xai-fast-worktree Filesystem, version control, execution, checkpoints — and fast git worktrees xai-codebase-graph Structural understanding of a repo, not just grep xai-grok-memory Memory is a subsystem, not a prompt trick xai-grok-mcp MCP is a first-class integration surface xai-grok-hooks, xai-hooks-plugins-types Hooks and plugins have their own type layer xai-grok-subagent-resolution Resolving which subagent handles what is hard enough to need its own crate xai-token-estimation Counting tokens before you spend them xai-hunk-tracker Tracking diff hunks across an editing session xai-grok-pager, xai-ratatui-inline The TUI — scrollback, prompts, modals, inline rendering xai-acp-lib Agent Client Protocol — editors embed the agent xai-grok-telemetry, xai-mixpanel Telemetry and product analytics, as first-class crates ptyctl, xai-tty-utils, xai-grok-crash-handler Terminals are hostile and processes crash Read that list again as a build plan. The naive mental model of a coding agent is "a loop that calls a model and runs tools." The actual decomposition includes a codebase graph, a memory subsystem, checkpointing, worktree management, hunk tracking, subagent resolution, token estimation, crash handling and a PTY control layer — before you write a single prompt. ★ The scale check. Simon Willison counted 844,530 lines of Rust in the tree, only ~3% of it vendored dependencies, and noted that OpenAI's Codex sits at roughly 950,933 lines. Two independent teams, converging near a million lines, for "a loop around an LLM." If your agent project feels like it's ballooning, this is the calibration: it is not you, and the hard part was never the loop. There's also a xai-grok-mermaid crate — a terminal renderer that draws Mermaid diagrams with Unicode box-drawing characters. It is not important. It is a nice reminder that shipping polish is a large fraction of any real agent. آخر تحقّق: 2026-07-16. تستشهد هذه الصفحة بحقائق تتغيّر مع الوقت — اعتبر التاريخ أعلاه دليلًا على حداثتها. تأكّد من المصدر الرسمي.
documents.s: The crate map is the real lesson

documents.t: This is where the repo stops being a textbook and starts being evidence. In July 2026 a researcher's wire capture showed Grok Build uploading entire repositories — full git history, never-read files, .env contents — to a Google Cloud Storage bucket, through a channel unrelated to what the model read. AILmanac covers that incident and the general failure mode in What your agent uploads. xAI disabled the behavior server-side and said the retained data would be deleted. The published source contains that machinery. Verifiable from the repo directly: crates/codegen/xai-grok-shell/src/upload/gcs.rs exists. crates/codegen/xai-file-utils/src/upload_config.rs defines DEDUP_GCS_PREFIX = "repo_changes_dedup". That constant is the interesting one. The researcher's intercepted upload went to object paths of the form gs://grok-code-session-traces/repo_changes_dedup/v2/…. The path prefix captured on the wire is a named constant in xAI's own published source. The same file defines both ARCHIVE_SCHEMA_VERSION (v2) and ARCHIVE_SCHEMA_VERSION_V3 — meaning the archive format had been iterated to a third version. This was maintained infrastructure, not a stray debug path. The module documentation in gcs.rs is blunter than any press statement. It refers to the upload helpers as "the data-collector helpers," and the file's entire reason for existing is an engineering fix: threading refresh-aware credentials through so that stale tokens stop causing POST /v1/storage 401s. Someone was debugging the reliability of the repository upload path as production work. Simon Willison reports that the upload path is now disabled in the published tree, returning a hard-coded error. That is consistent with xAI's stated position, and we were not able to independently confirm the specific mechanism by code search — treat it as reported rather than verified here. ★ What to take from this. Not "xAI is uniquely bad" — the wider lesson from the security page stands: this class of channel exists in some form in many agents, and reading the source is the only way to know. Take instead the meta-point: this is what source transparency is actually for. You cannot audit a binary's data flows in an afternoon. You can grep a published tree for bucket_url in about ten seconds. The release is genuinely valuable precisely because it makes the uncomfortable parts greppable. Check yourself 0/4 1xai-org/grok-build is Apache 2.0 licensed. What does that tell you about contributing a fix upstream? You can open a PR like any open-source projectNothing — the license grants usage rights, and CONTRIBUTING.md explicitly refuses external PRsYou must sign a CLA first, then contributeContributions are accepted only from xAI API customers 2The repo has two commits and a root SOURCE_REV file containing one hash. What does that mean? The project is only two days oldThe history was squashed to hide a security bugIt is a periodic export of an internal monorepo; SOURCE_REV points at the internal revision it was cut fromGit history is stored in the crates/ subdirectories 3Roughly how large is the Grok Build harness, and what's the comparable figure for OpenAI's Codex? ~30k lines vs ~40k lines~845k lines of Rust vs ~950k lines~5M lines vs ~6M lines~120k lines vs ~2M lines 4What does the DEDUP_GCS_PREFIX constant in upload_config.rs confirm? That the upload path is currently enabledThat the GCS object-path prefix seen in the researcher's wire capture is a named constant in xAI's own source — maintained infrastructure, not a stray debug pathThat user data was never uploadedThat the bucket is publicly readable
documents.s: The data-collector code is still in the tree

documents.t: Be honest about the constraints before you fork: Guided walkthrough1 of 4 1Read it for architecture, not for code⌄ The crate boundaries are the product of a well-funded team shipping to real users. That decomposition — tools split from tools-api, workspace from agent, subagent resolution as its own concern — is the transferable asset. Copying Rust out of it buys you far less than copying the shape. ←PreviousNext→ 2Treat the tool implementations as a survey⌄ Willison notes the tool implementations show signs of being adapted from competing products including Codex, Claude and Cursor. That makes the tool layer a convergent-design reference: where three or four agents independently landed on the same tool contract, that contract is probably right. ←PreviousNext→ 3Audit before you trust any agent, including this one⌄ The value of a published tree is that you can check claims instead of believing them. Grep for HTTP clients, bucket URLs, telemetry crates and upload call sites. xai-grok-telemetry and xai-mixpanel are first-class crates here — that is not a scandal, but it is a fact you can only learn by looking. ←PreviousNext→ 4Don't plan on upstreaming anything⌄ No PRs, no issues. If you fork, you own your fork forever, and you rebase against monorepo exports on xAI's schedule. Budget accordingly. ←PreviousNext→ If you want to explore the tree without building it: Clone and map the crate structure CopyOpen in Claude↗ git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/xai-org/grok-build cd grok-build # The inventory of what a production coding agent needs ls crates/codegen/ # Where does data leave the machine? Start here, not with the README. grep -rn "bucket_url\|/v1/storage\|upload_bytes" crates/ --include=*.rs | head -30 # Which internal revision was this cut from? cat SOURCE_REV

If you drive Claude Code, Grok Build is the same category of tool with its guts exposed — read it as a second opinion on problems you already have. Coding agent CLIs compared places it against the field, and Grok for Claude users covers the xAI ecosystem around it. For the architecture ideas the crate map gestures at, see long-running agent harnesses and agent memory architectures — xai-grok-memory and xai-grok-subagent-resolution are one team's answers to exactly those problems. And read What your agent uploads alongside this page. That one shows you how to catch a channel like this on the wire with mitmproxy and a canary repo. This one shows you what it looks like in the source. The two techniques together are the whole audit.

متوسط You already think in Claude. Then r/LocalLLaMA won't stop talking about Kimi K2 — a Chinese open-weight model that people keep calling "the open Claude for agents." A teammate wants to run it on their own hardware; a project needs weights it can actually download; someone hands you an OpenAI-shaped codebase and asks whether Moonshot is a cheaper backend. This page maps your Claude mental model onto Moonshot AI's Kimi K2 family, and — more usefully — tells you the handful of things about it that genuinely surprise people, each one sourced. What you'll learn Understand what Kimi K2 actually is: a 1-trillion-parameter sparse MoE with only 32B active per token Learn the three non-obvious things K2 does differently from a typical model release (native INT4 weights, 200–300-step tool chains, a truly permissive license) Know the K2 lineage — K2-Instruct, K2 Thinking, and the K2.x Code line — and which one to reach for Point a Claude-shaped or OpenAI-shaped codebase at Kimi in a few lines, and know when it beats reaching for Claude

Kimi K2 is an open-weight (downloadable, self-hostable), trillion-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model from Moonshot AI, tuned specifically for agentic tool use — long chains of "call a tool, read the result, decide the next move" — and released under a license permissive enough to use commercially. That "open-weight" part is the whole reason to care. Claude's weights never leave Anthropic; you rent the model through an API. Kimi K2's weights are on Hugging Face — you can download them, run them in your own data centre, fine-tune them, and inspect them. If your constraint is data can't leave our network or we need to own the model, that's a different category of tool than Claude, not a cheaper version of it. (For the Claude-side equivalents of self-hosting and hybrid setups, see Claude + local models and choosing a model.)
Most "new open model" pages just restate the benchmark table. Here are the parts that are actually non-obvious — the things most Claude users don't know until someone points them out.
documents.s: Three things about K2 that surprise people

documents.t: K2 is a sparse Mixture-of-Experts: 1 trillion total parameters, but only 32 billion activated per token. The router picks 8 experts out of 384 (plus one always-on shared expert) for each token. So the model has the knowledge capacity of a trillion-parameter network, but each forward pass only pays for ~32B of compute. Why this matters to you: "1T parameters" sounds like it needs a supercomputer, and to hold the weights it does (that's a lot of VRAM). But the inference cost per token tracks the 32B active count, not the trillion. This is the same architectural bet behind DeepSeek and Qwen's larger MoE models — see DeepSeek & Qwen open models for the family resemblance.
documents.s: 1. It's a trillion parameters, but only ~3% fire at once

documents.t: Normally you download a model in full precision and then quantize it yourself to make it fit, losing a little quality in the process. Kimi K2 Thinking flips that: Moonshot applied Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) during post-training, shipping the MoE weights natively in INT4. Because the model was trained to be INT4, the quantization is close to lossless — and Moonshot reports roughly 2× faster generation as a result. The practical upshot: the "small, fast" version isn't a degraded afterthought — it's the reference model. You're not choosing between "the real one" and "the quantized one." Pro tip Rule of thumb: an INT4 model needs roughly half a byte per parameter to hold the weights. A trillion-parameter INT4 model is still a serious multi-GPU deployment — 'open weight' does not mean 'runs on your laptop'. Budget accordingly, or rent it through a hosted endpoint.
documents.s: 2. The released weights are already INT4 — on purpose

documents.t: This is the number that made K2 Thinking a story. Moonshot reports the model holds coherent, goal-directed behaviour across up to 200–300 consecutive tool invocations — where, by their account, earlier agent systems tend to drift or lose the plot after 30–50 steps. If you've built agents, you know the failure mode: it's fine for ten steps, then forgets its own goal, repeats a tool call, or hallucinates a result. A model tuned to survive hundreds of steps is aimed squarely at the long-horizon agent — research loops, multi-file refactors, browse-then-synthesize tasks. It's the same problem Claude's agent tooling is built around, approached from the open-weight side. آخر تحقّق: 2026-07-15. Model versions, context sizes, and prices in the K2 line move fast (K2-Instruct, K2 Thinking, and the K2.5 → K2.6 → K2.7 Code releases all landed within months of each other). Benchmark numbers below are Moonshot's own reported figures for Kimi K2 Thinking; treat any specific score, price, or context length as a snapshot and check the linked source for the current release. تأكّد من المصدر الرسمي.
