documents.t: Artificial Analysis — مقارنات مستقلة ومحدّثة باستمرار للقدرة/السعر/السرعة عبر النماذج المفتوحة والطليعية (المكان الذي تعيد فيه فحص التفاصيل القابلة للتقادم). Anthropic — نظرة عامة على النماذج — تشكيلة Claude الراهنة وسياقها وقدراتها. Anthropic — تسعير الواجهة البرمجية — التكاليف الراهنة لكل توكِن لحساب أرقامك عند الحجم. Ollama · LM Studio — لتشغيل النماذج المفتوحة الأوزان محليًا لمسار المحلي/الهجين. Meta — Llama · Mistral — النماذج — عائلات مفتوحة الأوزان شائعة الاستخدام في الوكلاء المحليين.
ابنِ الجانب المحلي ← الوكلاء المحليون للذكاء الاصطناعي اربط الهجين ← Claude + النماذج المحلية أطّر الاختيار بشكل أوسع ← اختيار نموذج اجعل القرار قابلًا للقياس ← التقييمات

متوسط On September 22, 2026, Xiaomi published MiMo-V2.6 — three checkpoints on Hugging Face under a plain MIT license, headlined by a 1.02-trillion-parameter sparse Mixture-of-Experts model with a 1-million-token context that takes text, image, video and audio as input. It landed the same day as Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Sol/Luna, and it went straight to the top of Hacker News. The headline write-ups all say roughly the same thing: frontier-class open weights, twenty to sixty times cheaper than closed models. That part is true and easy to check. What nobody has written up is the part that decides whether you should actually use it — which benchmark versions the wins came from, why the flagship is not a machine you own, and what the third price tier is for. What you'll learn Read the MiMo-V2.6 benchmark table the way its own model card reports it — including the 14-point Terminal-Bench 4.0 deficit the press coverage did not quote Know why a 33-point generational jump on an agentic benchmark usually means the old model could not drive the harness, not that the new one got smarter Understand the architecture that buys the 1M context: 384 experts with 8 active, and a 6:1 sliding-window-to-global attention ratio Pick between Pro, Flash and the 9B distill by what hardware you actually have — Pro's own launch command wants two nodes See what the 10x-priced UltraSpeed tier sells you (latency, from the same weights) and when that is worth paying for آخر تحقّق: 2026-09-23. Architecture, license, benchmark scores and serving commands here are read from the Hugging Face model card published at launch. Hosted pricing is as reported by launch coverage of the OpenRouter and Xiaomi AI Studio listings; per-token prices move faster than anything else on this page — check the live listing before you budget against it. تأكّد من المصدر الرسمي.

MiMo-V2.6-Pro is an MIT-licensed, 1.02T-total / 42B-active sparse MoE with a 1M-token context and text, image, video and audio input that ties or beats Claude Opus 5 on short-horizon agentic and automation benchmarks, trails it badly on long-horizon terminal work, and costs roughly one-tenth as much per token when you rent it instead of running it.

This is the one to internalise. Launch coverage widely reported MiMo-V2.6-Pro at 89.9 on Terminal Bench 2.1, just ahead of Claude Opus 5's 89.1. Xiaomi's own model card does not report Terminal Bench 2.1 at all. It reports Terminal Bench 4.0, where MiMo-V2.6-Pro scores 34.9 against Opus 5's 49.0 — a 14.1-point deficit. Both numbers are real. Terminal Bench 2.1 is an older, largely saturated harness where every frontier model clusters near 90 and a 0.8-point gap is noise. Terminal Bench 4.0 is the current one, and it is where models are still spread out. If you read "beats Claude on Terminal Bench" anywhere, the first question is always which version — because on agentic suites the version change is usually a bigger effect than the model change. The same pattern shows up in AILmanac's coverage of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and Gemini 3.8 Flash: parity on DeepSWE, a 15–20 point hole on Terminal-Bench 4.0. It is becoming the signature shape of the cheap tier.
documents.s: 1. The Terminal-Bench win and the Terminal-Bench loss are the same model

documents.t: The model card's own table includes the previous generation. MiMo-V2.5-Pro scored 19.0 on DeepSWE v1.1 and 1.5 on Terminal Bench 4.0. V2.6-Pro scores 71.9 and 34.9. A model does not get 23× better at terminal work in one generation. A score of 1.5 means the old model essentially could not complete the benchmark's tool-call protocol — it was failing at the harness, not at the reasoning. Read enormous generational deltas on agentic benchmarks as "we fixed tool calling" first, and only then as capability. The deltas on non-agentic benchmarks are the honest ones: ProgramBench went 12.5 → 26.5, roughly a doubling, which is a large but believable generational step.
documents.s: 2. A 33-point generational jump is a harness story, not an intelligence story

documents.t: MiMo-V2.6-Pro's LLM backbone is 70 layers: 60 sliding-window attention, 10 global attention — a 6:1 ratio. Sliding-window layers only keep a local KV window, so the per-token KV footprint at 1M tokens is a fraction of what a fully global 70-layer stack would need. The ten global layers are what still let information travel end to end. The MoE is 384 routed experts with 8 active per token, giving 42B active out of 1.02T — about 4.1% of the model runs on any given token. Flash uses the same shape at 309–311B total and ~15B active. This is why a trillion-parameter model can be served at all: you pay 1T in memory and 42B in compute. On top of that sits a 5-layer multi-token-prediction speculative decoder that drafts 7 tokens per pass. That is a throughput mechanism, and it matters for the next point.
documents.s: 3. The 1M context is bought with attention layout, not brute force

documents.t: Two things the marketing language blurs: Modalities are input-side. The card lists text, image, video and audio as modalities, with a 681M-parameter MiMo ViT vision encoder and a 308M AudioTokenizer plus a 127M audio patch encoder. The Hugging Face pipeline tag for Pro is text generation. You can feed it a video and ask questions; it answers in text. It is not a speech or image generator. If you want generation across media, that is a different page: generative media. UltraSpeed is the same model at 10× the price. MiMo-V2.6-Pro-UltraSpeed is described as Pro quality at up to 20× the output speed, listed at roughly ten times Pro's per-token price. There is no separate set of weights on Hugging Face for it — it is a serving tier built on the speculative decoder and Xiaomi's infrastructure. That is a perfectly reasonable product, but price it as what it is: you are buying tokens-per-second for interactive and real-time workloads, not accuracy. If your job is a background batch, UltraSpeed is a 10× overpay.
documents.s: 4. "Omnimodal" means omnimodal in, and UltraSpeed sells latency, not quality

documents.t: All figures below are Xiaomi's own runs, from the MiMo-V2.6-Pro-RL model card. No independent replication existed at the time of writing. Benchmark MiMo-V2.6 Pro MiMo-V2.6 Flash MiMo-V2.5 Pro Claude Opus 5 GPT-5.6 Sol Claude Fable 5 DeepSWE v1.1 71.9 67.9 19.0 74.0 73.0 70.0 ProgramBench 26.5 26.0 12.5 37.0 25.0 33.0 MiMo Code Bench 63.2 61.2 40.4 68.6 59.3 — AutomationBench v1.0.6 53.1 52.3 16.0 50.3 45.8 46.2 Toolathlon-Verified 76.9 73.6 49.1 80.6 74.9 77.9 Terminal Bench 4.0 34.9 28.8 1.5 49.0 39.9 42.4 OSWorld-Verified 82.0 80.8 — 83.4 83.0 86.0 CyberGym 94.0 95.1 40.0 — — — MiMo VisualCoding 72.3 71.5 — 70.0 73.4 69.1 Three readings worth having: Flash is within a few points of Pro almost everywhere. 67.9 vs 71.9 on DeepSWE, 52.3 vs 53.1 on AutomationBench, and it beats Pro on CyberGym. At roughly a third of Pro's hosted price and a third of the parameters, Flash is the default unless you have measured a reason otherwise. The competitor columns for CyberGym are empty. Xiaomi reported 94.0 and 95.1 and published no Claude or GPT comparison. Treat an unopposed number as unopposed — it tells you the model is competent at the task, not that it leads. Pro wins exactly one row outright: AutomationBench. Everything else is a near-tie or a loss. "Frontier-class open weights" is fair; "beats Claude" is not. On the aggregate side, Artificial Analysis' Intelligence Index v4.3 placed MiMo-V2.6-Pro at roughly 46, reported as first among open-weight models and level with Grok 4.7, against about 53 for the closed frontier. A seven-point index gap for a tenth of the price is the actual pitch.

documents.t: Rented, as reported at launch from the OpenRouter and Xiaomi listings, per million tokens: Model Input Output MiMo-V2.6-Flash $0.14 $0.28 MiMo-V2.6-Pro $0.435 $0.87 MiMo-V2.6-Pro-UltraSpeed $4.35 $8.70 For scale, Claude Opus 5.5 lists at $4 / $20 (see the Opus 5.5 field guide). Pro is roughly 9× cheaper on input and 23× cheaper on output. UltraSpeed costs about the same as Opus 5.5 on input and less than half on output — which is the honest way to think about that tier. Owned is a different conversation, and the launch commands give it away. The model card's SGLang example for Pro asks for --tp 16 --dp 2 ... --nnodes 2: tensor parallelism across sixteen devices, two data-parallel replicas, two nodes. That is a rack, not a workstation. The vLLM path is lighter at --tensor-parallel-size 8, still eight accelerators for a 1.02T checkpoint in BF16. Flash, at ~309–311B total and ~15B active, is the variant that a serious single-node box can plausibly serve. The MiMo-V2.6-Distill-Qwen-9B checkpoint — a 9B distillation, listed on Hugging Face under image-text-to-text — is the one that fits on a laptop-class GPU. If your goal is "run a capable open model at home", start there and at Run models locally with Ollama, not at Pro. One more ownership caveat: the repositories published are the post-RL checkpoints (-Pro-RL, -Flash-RL). No base checkpoint was released. You can serve, quantise and adapt these, but you cannot start your own post-training from the pre-RL base.

documents.t: Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Decide input-side first⌄ If your workload never sends an image, video or audio clip, most of what makes MiMo-V2.6 distinctive is irrelevant to you and a cheaper text-only open model may match it. The omnimodal encoders are the differentiator — use them or discount them. ←PreviousNext→ 2Start on Flash, not Pro⌄ Flash is within a few points of Pro on every published row and ahead on one, at roughly a third of the price. Run your real workload on Flash first. Only escalate to Pro if you can measure the gap on your own task. ←PreviousNext→ 3Re-run the benchmark that matches your shape of work⌄ Short, bounded, tool-using tasks (AutomationBench, Toolathlon) are where MiMo is strong. Long autonomous terminal sessions (Terminal Bench 4.0) are where it is 14 points behind. Build a 20-task private eval in the shape you actually ship, and score it yourself. ←PreviousNext→ 4Test the 1M context at your real length⌄ Sixty of seventy layers are sliding-window. Long-range retrieval rides on ten global layers. Run needle-in-a-haystack and multi-hop retrieval at the context length you will really use before you trust the ceiling. ←PreviousNext→ 5Price the tier, not the model⌄ Flash, Pro and Pro-UltraSpeed are a 1x / 3x / 31x price ladder over the same family. Decide whether you are buying accuracy (Flash to Pro) or latency (Pro to UltraSpeed) — they are different purchases. ←PreviousNext→ Call MiMo-V2.6-Flash through an OpenAI-compatible endpoint CopyOpen in Claude↗ curl https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPENROUTER_API_KEY" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "xiaomi/mimo-v2.6-flash", "messages": [ {"role": "user", "content": "Summarise the failure modes in this log and propose one fix."} ] }' Serve MiMo-V2.6-Pro with vLLM (the model card's own launch line) CopyOpen in Claude↗ vllm serve XiaomiMiMo/MiMo-V2.6-Pro-RL \ --tensor-parallel-size 8 \ --trust-remote-code \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.95 \ --max-model-len auto \ --reasoning-parser mimo \ --tool-call-parser mimo \ --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --generation-config vllm Pro tip Note the two parser flags: --reasoning-parser mimo and --tool-call-parser mimo. MiMo emits its reasoning and tool calls in a family-specific format. Omit these and your serving stack will hand the raw markers back to your application as ordinary text — a silent failure that looks like the model ignoring your tools. --trust-remote-code is required because the modelling code ships with the checkpoint. Read it before you run it on anything you care about; that flag executes vendor Python in your serving process. The SGLang path adds EAGLE speculative-decoding flags. That is where the throughput advantage lives — a vanilla launch leaves the multi-token predictor unused.
documents.s: How to evaluate it for your own work

documents.t: Good fit High-volume classification, extraction or automation over mixed media, where $0.14/M input changes what is economically possible at all. Anything you must run on your own hardware for privacy or jurisdiction reasons and that needs vision or audio understanding — few MIT-licensed models offer that combination. See a private local AI stack. Short, bounded agentic tasks with well-specified tools, which is where AutomationBench and Toolathlon scores say it is genuinely competitive. Poor fit Long autonomous coding sessions. The Terminal Bench 4.0 gap is 14 points against Opus 5 and 5 points against GPT-5.6 Sol, and it is the vendor's own number. Anywhere you need a base checkpoint to post-train from. Only RL checkpoints shipped. Single-box self-hosting of Pro. Budget for Flash or the 9B distill, or rent Pro.
documents.s: When to reach for it, and when not

documents.t: Worth noting because it is unusually specific: Xiaomi published the RL training run's shape and cost — roughly a six-day run, 30 RL steps, about 750,000 trajectories, 1,568 prompts with 16 rollouts per step, at a reported ~$2.62M for Pro and ~$850K for Flash, using asynchronous GRPO with the MoE router frozen during RL. Two things to take from it. First, a frozen router during reinforcement learning is a stability choice: it keeps expert assignment fixed so the policy update cannot quietly reshape which experts fire. Second, and more useful: a frontier-adjacent post-training run now costs single-digit millions, not hundreds. That is the number that explains why four labs shipped in the same week. Check yourself 0/5 1Press coverage said MiMo-V2.6-Pro beat Claude Opus 5 on Terminal Bench; the model card shows it 14 points behind. What explains the contradiction? The press used a different model variantThe two figures are from different Terminal Bench versions — 2.1 (saturated, near-90 scores) versus 4.0 (current, spread out)The press quoted Flash, not ProOne of the two numbers is fabricated 2MiMo-V2.5-Pro scored 1.5 on Terminal Bench 4.0; V2.6-Pro scores 34.9. What is the most likely reading? The new model is roughly 23 times more intelligentThe benchmark was made easier between runsThe previous generation largely could not drive the benchmark's tool-call protocol, so the jump is mostly harness compatibilityThe old score was a typo 3What does the MiMo-V2.6-Pro-UltraSpeed tier actually sell at roughly 10x Pro's price? متوسط On August 3, 2026 MiniMax pushed the weights of MiniMax-H3 (consumer name: Hailuo 3.0) to Hugging Face — a 33-billion-parameter, single-stream Transformer that turns text, images, video and audio references into 4–15 second clips at up to 2K/24fps with native stereo audio, all generated in one pass. That last part is the interesting one: there is no separate TTS stage, no bolted-on SFX pipeline. Dialogue, room tone and picture come out together, from the same model. Three days earlier the paid API had opened at $0.1625/second for 2K (~$9.75/minute of video), roughly half the cost of Kling 3.0 or Seedance 2.0 at comparable resolution. On the Artificial Analysis leaderboards single-run scores put H3 #1 in video editing with audio, top-three in text-to-video and image-to-video. That combination — frontier-tier video quality, open weights, and honest sub-$10/minute pricing — is what put H3 on every generative-media feed this week. This page is what most other write-ups miss: the parts that determine whether H3 is actually useful to you. What you'll learn Understand the H3 architecture — single-stream Transformer, H3-VAE, MM-RoPE — and why it produces video and audio in one forward pass Know the three self-hosting gotchas nobody puts on the landing page: the geo-restricted license, the 768p ceiling on the open base, and the AdaLN parameter-skip trick Get a working self-hosted path: minimum 42.5 GB of weights, quantization choices, and how a 12 GB card runs it with offloading Try H3 from the API with a real cURL you can copy, and know the input-shape limits (12 files max, ≤64 MB body, public URLs only) Pick between H3 and the closed alternatives (Kling 3.0, Seedance 2.0, Veo, Sora) with clear tie-breakers on price, control and licensing آخر تحقّق: 2026-08-08. Video-model prices, license terms and quantized checkpoints churn weekly in this space. Anything with a dollar sign, a GB count or a benchmark rank on this page is a snapshot — re-check the official model card and the vendor's pricing page before you commit. The architecture facts (33B / single-stream / MM-RoPE / native audio) are the durable part. تأكّد من المصدر الرسمي.

documents.t: The Hugging Face model card links a MiniMax H3 Community License Agreement whose text is application-gated for four regions: the United States, the European Union, the United Kingdom and the Republic of Korea. In practice that means: if you or your organisation is in any of those places and you want to run H3 on your own hardware (or serve it to your users), you need to complete the H3 licence application at platform.minimax.io/h3-license first. The restriction extends to outputs, not just the weights — a detail most reblog posts skip. If you are outside those regions the standard Community License applies. If you are in them, treat the API as your default path until your application clears, or use the license reviewer at your org before shipping anything that touches the weights. This is a real, enforceable restriction — not the usual "please don't do bad things" clause.
documents.s: 1. The Community License blocks self-hosting in the US, EU, UK and South Korea

documents.t: Every "up to 2K" headline about H3 elides a key detail: the open-weight base models (Base FL2VA for text-to-video / first-last-frame, Base Ref2VA for multi-reference) generate at 768p. The 2K output people are marveling at on the Hailuo app comes from H3-Regenerate-2K, an in-context upsampler that runs after the base model and that MiniMax has not open-sourced. H3-Context-IR, the multimodal instruction preprocessor, is also API-only. The consequence for self-hosters is simple: you get the same generation quality the frontier system is built on, but you top out at 768p unless you chain your own upscaler (Topaz, ESRGAN, a diffusion upsampler) after the fact. This is fine for many use cases — 768p at 24fps is more than enough for social clips, storyboards, and rapid iteration — but it's not the same product as the paid tier.
documents.s: 2. The open base tops out at 768p — 2K only exists inside the API

documents.t: The model card breaks the H3-Omni-Transformer down as a 33 B dense single-stream Transformer of which roughly 13 B parameters live in AdaLN-related branches. AdaLN (Adaptive Layer Norm) is how diffusion-style transformers absorb conditioning signals (timestep, class, text embedding) — and its outputs, per conditioning slot, are precomputable. That's how third-party providers hit a minimum 42.5 GB working configuration even though naive BF16 weights are much larger: they combine a pruned INT8 checkpoint (~20 GB) with an NVFP4 AWQ text encoder (~16 GB) and both VAEs (~5.8 GB), and skip the cached-branch weights at inference time. The rule of thumb from the ComfyUI ecosystem: a 12 GB card can run H3 with CPU/RAM offloading, at the cost of longer render times per clip. If you have 24 GB or more, offload isn't needed.
documents.s: 3. About 13 B of the 33 B parameters are AdaLN branches you can precompute and skip

documents.t: H3 is a single-stream, modality-agnostic Transformer. There is one attention stack, one FFN stack, and video/audio/text tokens all pass through it. The four components you actually load are: Component Role Open-sourced? H3-Omni-Transformer 33 B dense generator (video + audio) ✅ (BF16, INT8, pruned INT8) H3-Encoder Multimodal text/vision encoder — reuses Qwen3-VL-32B layer-50 hidden states ✅ H3-VisualVAE Temporal-causal video autoencoder, f16t4d24 compression ✅ H3-AudioVAE Stereo audio, 32 kHz output, 40 Hz temporal rate ✅ H3-Context-IR Multimodal instruction preprocessor ❌ API-only H3-Regenerate-2K In-context upscaler to 2K ❌ API-only Two design choices are worth calling out for anyone comparing H3 to other video models: 3-D MM-RoPE positional embeddings. Rotary positions are extended to three axes (spatial x, spatial y, time), so temporal coherence is baked into the attention pattern rather than added by a separate temporal module. This is one of the main reasons H3 keeps subject identity and lighting stable across 15-second clips. H3-VAE gives a 4× effective sequence-length gain. The custom tokenizer packs more pixels per token than the standard VAEs used by prior open video models — that's what makes 2K output tractable at all in this parameter class. The native audio pass is the other differentiator. Because dialogue, SFX and room tone are generated in the same forward pass as picture, lip-sync and diegetic audio come out coherent by default. Reference audio (WAV/MP3, 2–15s per clip, up to 3 clips) enables voice cloning; but audio references must accompany an image or video reference — the API rejects audio-only inputs.
documents.s: What H3 actually is (the architecture in one page)

documents.t: If you're planning to run H3 locally, these are the numbers that determine what fits: Checkpoint Diffusion model Text encoder Both VAEs Minimum working total BF16 (reference) 61.7 GB 48.0 GB 5.82 GB ~115 GB INT8 31.7 GB 25.3 GB 5.82 GB ~63 GB Pruned INT8 + NVFP4 AWQ TE 19.5 GB 14.6 GB 5.82 GB ~42.5 GB VRAM: 24 GB comfortably, 12 GB with offload (slower per clip). SGLang example configs use 4 GPUs for serving. Pull the latest and the new H3 nodes appear automatically. ←PreviousNext→ 2Pick a checkpoint that fits your VRAM⌄ 24 GB+ card → INT8 or BF16. 12–16 GB card → pruned INT8 + NVFP4 AWQ text encoder + CPU offload. Below 12 GB, use the API — you won't have a good time. ←PreviousNext→ 3Load one of the six official workflow templates⌄ Three local (text-to-video, image-to-video, reference-to-video) and three API-backed (text-to-video, reference-to-video, first/last-frame-to-video) ship in ComfyUI's built-in gallery. The API is REST + polling. You post a job, receive a task_id, and poll a query endpoint until status == "succeeded". Only public URLs work — Base64 payloads are rejected, and the total request body is capped at 64 MB. Reference limits: ≤9 images, ≤3 video clips, ≤3 audio clips, 12 files total, ≤7 000-character prompt. H3 text-to-video with a voice reference (Python) CopyOpen in Claude↗ import os, time, requests headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['MINIMAX_API_KEY']}"} payload = { "model": "MiniMax-H3", "content": [ {"type": "text", "text": "Wide shot: a lighthouse keeper walks onto the balcony and says, 'Follow the wind, live free.' Voice follows reference audio 1."}, {"type": "audio_url", "audio_url": {"url": "https://example.com/voice-ref.mp3"}, "role": "reference_audio"}, {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": "https://example.com/lighthouse.jpg"}, "role": "reference_image"}, ], "resolution": "2K", # 2K is the only value the API accepts right now "duration": 8, # seconds, 4–15 "ratio": "16:9", } task_id = requests.post( "https://api.minimax.io/v2/video_generation", headers=headers, json=payload, ).json()["task_id"] while True: time.sleep(10) task = requests.get( f"https://api.minimax.io/v2/query/video_generation/{task_id}", headers=headers, ).json()["task"] if task["status"] == "succeeded": print(task["video_url"]) break if task["status"] == "failed": raise RuntimeError(task) H3 locally via diffusers (self-host, 768p) CopyOpen in Claude↗ from diffusers import DiffusionPipeline import torch pipe = DiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained( "MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-H3", dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map="cuda", ) video, audio = pipe( prompt="Slow dolly-in on a neon-lit ramen shop at night; steam rising; jazz sax outside.", num_frames=24 * 8, # 8 seconds at 24 fps height=768, width=1344, generator=torch.manual_seed(42), ) video.save("ramen.mp4"); audio.save("ramen.wav")

متوسط Once your product does more than one kind of thing, one model stops being the right answer for every request. Classify the ticket, extract the fields, draft the reply, review it — those are four jobs with four different cost/latency/quality budgets. The pattern the whole field has converged on in 2026 is to route each request to the model that fits the job, and to escalate when the cheap model isn't good enough. This page is the editorial guide to those patterns: what they are, when each one ships, the recipes that work, and the failure modes to avoid. What you'll learn Know the six routing patterns that ship in production and when to reach for each Understand the difference between routing (one decision up front) and cascading (escalate on failure) Build your first classifier router with a copy-paste prompt and a one-week rollout plan Read the cost math: when routing saves real money, and when the overhead eats the savings Recognize the anti-patterns that turn a router into an outage waiting to happen آخر تحقّق: 2026-08-10. Anthropic's own "Building Effective Agents" guide defines Routing as a first-class workflow: "Routing classifies an input and directs it to a specialized followup task. This workflow allows for separation of concerns, and building more specialized prompts." Two of the examples they give are exactly the ones covered here — splitting customer-service categories into distinct downstream flows, and "routing easy questions to smaller models like Claude Haiku... and difficult ones to Claude Sonnet." Model names, prices and quality gaps drift; always check the current per-provider docs before hard-coding a threshold. documents.s: Model Routing Patterns: Cascades, Classifiers, and What Actually Ships

documents.t: The "one big model for everything" era is quietly over. Three forces drove the shift: A wide, well-behaved price curve. Every major provider now ships a family — Anthropic (Haiku / Sonnet / Opus), OpenAI (small / mid / frontier), Google (Flash / Pro), plus open-weight tiers. Cheap tiers are 10–100× cheaper than the frontier and, on narrow tasks, only marginally worse. Leaving the cheap tier idle is money you're setting on fire. Real latency budgets. A classify step in front of a support agent needs to answer in under 300 ms. A frontier model is often the wrong tool for reasons other than cost — it's just too slow for the step. Specialization. Different models genuinely lead on different tasks — one is better at structured JSON, another at long context, another at code, another at multilingual. The rankings shuffle monthly (see Choosing a Model), but the shape — "different tools for different jobs" — is durable. The result: a router in front of your models, deciding per-request where to send the work. The rest of this page is the design vocabulary for that router.
documents.s: Why routing is the default pattern in 2026

documents.t: Almost every pattern below is a variation on two ideas. Get the difference right and the rest is naming. Routing makes one decision up front, before any model runs. A classifier (a rule, a small model, or a bigger model) reads the request, picks a target, and hands off. Fast, cheap in the steady state, but wrong when the classifier is wrong — and you don't find out until later. Cascading runs the cheap model first and escalates to a stronger one only when a defined signal says "this answer isn't good enough." Robust because the signal is grounded in the actual output, but every escalation pays both models — so the win only survives when the cheap tier handles most traffic on its own. They compose. A production system usually does both: route to the right lane based on task type, then cascade inside a lane based on the cheap model's confidence. Anthropic's taxonomy calls the up-front decision "Routing" and the dynamic decomposition "Orchestrator-Workers"; cascading is the industry name for the "try small first, escalate on failure" variant of the same idea.
documents.s: The two big families: routing vs cascading

documents.t: A hand-written rule (regex, keyword, request field, message length) decides the target. No model runs to make the decision. When it wins. The signal is unambiguous and cheap: "if the request contains a code fence, send to the coding model", "if the customer is on the Enterprise plan, send to the frontier tier", "if the input is > 200k tokens, send to the long-context model." When it breaks. The rule silently rots as the domain shifts — new phrasing, new intents, edge cases the regex never anticipated. Every "if X then Y" is a small piece of tech debt. Ship it when. You have one or two high-value carve-outs (a paying tier, a code path, a language) and want zero latency overhead.

A small, fast model reads the request and returns a label — "billing" | "technical" | "sales" | "other" — which picks the downstream handler. Anthropic gives this as one of their canonical examples: easy questions to Haiku, hard ones to Sonnet. When it wins. You have a small, stable set of categories and each one deserves its own prompt/tool set/model. A single specialized prompt per category beats one giant do-everything system prompt. When it breaks. Categories overlap (many real requests are "billing and technical"), the classifier misroutes silently, or your label set explodes past ~10 categories and picks become noisy. Ship it when. You can enumerate the top 5–8 request types and each one materially benefits from a different handler. Classifier-router prompt (portable across Claude/GPT/Gemini) CopyOpen in Claude↗ You are a request classifier for a support product. Read the CUSTOMER MESSAGE below and return a JSON object with: - "category": one of ["billing", "technical", "account", "sales", "other"] - "confidence": a number from 0.0 to 1.0 - "reason": one short sentence explaining the pick If you are less than 0.7 confident, use "other" and say why. Return ONLY the JSON, no prose, no code fence. CUSTOMER MESSAGE: """ {{message}} """

Instead of what the request is about, you estimate how hard it is — length, entity count, whether it references numbers/code, whether tool use is likely — and pick a tier accordingly: cheap for easy, mid for medium, frontier for hard. When it wins. The task type is roughly homogeneous (say, "answer a coding question") but the individual requests vary wildly in difficulty. Instead of paying frontier prices for a two-line syntax question, you pay Haiku prices for those and reserve the frontier for the multi-file refactors. When it breaks. The "difficulty score" is really "prompt length", and long prompts aren't always hard prompts. A user pastes a huge stack trace and asks a trivial question about it — your router upgrades needlessly. Ship it when. You have measurable variance in difficulty within a task type and clear signals (length, presence of code, number of subquestions) that correlate with it.

Try the cheap model first. Check the answer against a failure signal. If it fails, retry on the stronger model. This is the pattern the industry ships more than any other, because the "signal" is grounded in what the model actually said — not a guess about what it will say. What counts as a signal? Anything cheap and reliable: schema validation on JSON output, a "does this answer the question?" check by an LLM judge, an explicit "needs_help": true field the model can emit when unsure, a downstream test that runs the code, a low logprob on the answer token when the provider exposes it. Cost math. The savings survive only when the cheap tier handles most traffic. If 90% of requests get resolved by the cheap model and 10% escalate, you pay 0.9 × cheap + 0.1 × (cheap + strong) ≈ mostly cheap. If half escalate, you're paying more than always using the strong model. When it wins. Tasks with a clear "did this work?" signal — code that runs or doesn't, JSON that validates or doesn't, extraction where the field either matches the source or doesn't. When it breaks. No cheap failure signal, or the cheap model thinks it succeeded when it didn't (silent failure — the worst case). Ship it when. You can name the failure signal in one sentence and it doesn't require the strong model to check.

Run the same request against N models in parallel and reconcile the answers — take a majority vote, take the first schema-valid one, or send all N to a judge model that picks the best. When it wins. Quality matters more than cost or latency: legal research, medical summarization, high-stakes financial extraction, "review this contract for red flags." Also useful for hard math and code, where different models make different mistakes and their intersection is more reliable than any single one. When it breaks. You pay N× the cost and inherit the slowest model's latency for every request. Ensembles are a tax you accept for quality, not a way to save money. Ship it when. The cost of getting the answer wrong is at least an order of magnitude larger than the cost of N model calls — which is almost never true for consumer traffic and often true for enterprise workflows.

Try the primary; on 429/5xx/timeout, transparently retry on a secondary from a different provider. This is the pattern every serious multi-model app needs even if it uses none of the others. When it wins. Every time your primary provider has an outage or throttles you at exactly the wrong moment. Fallback is a reliability pattern, not a cost-optimization pattern — the secondary is usually a different provider's equivalent tier, not a cheaper model. What to watch. The fallback path is untested code most of the time; it will regress. Run at least a small share of live traffic through the secondary continuously so you find out the response shape drifted before you're relying on it in an outage. Ship it when. Your uptime SLO is higher than any single provider's, or a single-provider dependency is a business risk (contracts, region availability, geopolitics).

Pattern Decision made Adds latency? Adds cost? Main risk Rule-based Before the model runs No No Rules silently rot as inputs shift Classifier Before, by a small model + one fast call + one cheap call Misroutes when categories overlap Complexity-based Before, by a heuristic Negligible Negligible "Difficulty" often means "length" Cascade After the cheap model tries + retry when escalating Mostly-cheap in steady state Silent success on wrong answer Ensemble Runs N in parallel, reconciles Slowest-of-N N× You are buying quality, not saving money Fallback Only on primary failure 0 in the happy path 0 in the happy path Untested until it matters

The patterns above are Lego. In production they compose. Three recipes we see repeatedly: Customer support agent. Classifier router picks a lane (billing / technical / account / sales), each lane has its own system prompt and tool set, inside the technical lane a cascade tries a cheap model first and escalates to the frontier when a "needs escalation" tool call fires. Fallback across providers wraps everything. Result: 70–90% of traffic never touches the frontier model. Coding assistant. Rule-based routing on file type and diff size sends small edits to a cheap tier and multi-file refactors to a coding-specialist. A cascade on the output — "does the patch apply cleanly and pass the smoke test?" — escalates failures to a stronger model. Compare against the field guide in Claude vs GPT vs Gemini for coding. RAG QA over a document corpus. Classifier picks between "answer from context" (cheap) and "needs cross-document reasoning" (mid). An ensemble of two models cross-checks the answer for high-stakes documents (contracts, filings). Compare with Retrieval-Augmented Generation.

Guided walkthrough1 of 7 1Day 1 — Pick one workload and log a week of it⌄ Instrument the *real* prompts your product already sends. You need at least a few hundred, ideally categorized by outcome (resolved / escalated / wrong). Without ground-truth traffic you're guessing at where the router should send things. ←PreviousNext→ 2Day 2 — Cluster by hand⌄ Read 100 requests and write down the 5–8 categories they naturally fall into. If you can't do this in an afternoon, the workload isn't ready for a classifier router — start with rule-based routing on the one or two obvious carve-outs (paying tier, long context, code). ←PreviousNext→ 3Day 3 — Write the classifier prompt⌄ Use the PromptCard above. Run it against yesterday's clusters on a cheap model (Haiku, Gemini Flash, GPT-nano). Measure accuracy against your hand-labels. If it's below ~85%, either merge categories or add few-shot examples — don't ship a router that's wrong 1-in-5. ←PreviousNext→ 4Day 4 — Route + shadow-log⌄ Wire the router into the request path but do NOT change the downstream model yet — every request still goes to the current model, and you *also* log where the router *would* have sent it. Compare against real outcomes for a day. ←PreviousNext→ 5Day 5 — Turn it on for one lane⌄ Flip routing live for the highest-value lane (usually the easiest one, where cheap-tier savings are biggest). Watch quality metrics — retry rate, thumbs-down rate, escalation rate — for 24 hours. ←PreviousNext→ 6Day 6 — Add a cascade inside a lane⌄ For the lane where the cheap tier is 'usually right but sometimes wrong', add an escalation signal (schema validation, judge check, explicit `needs_help` flag) and retry on the strong model. Confirm the fallback path with a chaos test — kill the cheap model and check the escalation works. ←PreviousNext→ 7Day 7 — Write the runbook and hand it off⌄ Document the router's rules, the classifier prompt, the escalation signal, and — critically — the metrics dashboard. If the router silently misroutes a category next month, someone needs to notice. ←PreviousNext→

documents.t: Cascades ship far more than learned routers. Research systems like RouteLLM train a router on preference data and can cut cost 2× or more on standard benchmarks (see the RouteLLM paper) — but training and maintaining a learned router is real engineering. Most teams get most of the wins from cheap-first + explicit escalation. The classifier is almost always a cheap chat model, not a fine-tune. Haiku-class or Flash-class models with a good prompt hit the accuracy bar for 5–8 categories. Fine-tune only if you're at scale and the cheap classifier is your bottleneck. The evaluator matters more than the router. A router without a metrics loop is a guess. Instrument every routing decision with request → chosen model → outcome, and review weekly. You can't tune what you don't measure. Infrastructure and design are separable. The patterns above are language- and provider-neutral. The plumbing — one endpoint per provider, virtual keys, per-team spend caps, prompt caching — is what an AI gateway gives you. Once you know the pattern you want, see AI gateways: LiteLLM, OpenRouter, Portkey, Vercel for the concrete choice.
documents.s: What actually gets deployed (2026 field notes)

documents.t: The classifier that calls the frontier model. If picking a lane costs as much as running the strong model would have, you saved nothing and added latency. Classifiers must be cheap. Cascade without a failure signal. "The cheap model returned something, so we're done" is not a signal — it's a bet. Every cascade needs a defined check the cheap model can fail. Rule proliferation. Ten rules is manageable. A hundred is a hand-coded classifier without the tests. When your rule set drifts past ~15 branches, rip it out and use a small model. Ensembles as a cost strategy. Running three models in parallel to save money is a category error — ensembles cost N× to buy quality, not to save cost. If you're using an ensemble to make up for a bad primary model, fix the primary instead. No fallback path. Every model provider goes down eventually. A single-provider product will inherit that outage. See AI gateways for the plumbing. Routing without observability. A router that quietly sends everything to the wrong lane looks fine until quality craters two weeks later. Log every decision with the input hash, the chosen model, the outcome, and the cost — and review weekly.

Check yourself 0/3 1You have a support product where 90% of requests are answered correctly by a cheap model, but the remaining 10% need the frontier. What pattern gives you the biggest cost win? Ensemble — run cheap + frontier in parallel and take the better oneCascade — try cheap first, escalate to frontier on a failure signalAlways route to the frontier, since 10% need it anywayFallback — send to cheap, then to frontier when cheap has an outage 2Anthropic's 'Building Effective Agents' guide defines Routing as: Running the same request against multiple models and voting on the answerClassifying an input and directing it to a specialized followup taskFailing over to a secondary provider when the primary is downEscalating to a stronger model when the cheap one returns low confidence 3You're building a classifier router. Your classifier prompt runs on a frontier model because 'accuracy matters'. What's the problem? Nothing — accuracy is what matters, so pay for itThe classifier now costs as much as the downstream work — you've paid for the routing decision without saving anything, and added latency on topFrontier models are less accurate at classification than cheaper modelsThe classifier must always be a fine-tuned model, not a chat model

Pick a target: Choosing a Model — the archetype framework the router leans on. Wire it up: AI gateways: LiteLLM, OpenRouter, Portkey, Vercel — the plumbing every router needs. Move a prompt to the model you routed to: Porting Prompts Across Models. Coding-specific routing signals: Claude vs GPT vs Gemini for coding. A purpose-built classifier stage: System One decision models: Jev, Kev and the open clones — calibrated probabilities in under half a second, and how to threshold them honestly. Anthropic's canonical workflow taxonomy: Building Effective Agents.

Anthropic — Building Effective Agents — canonical definitions of the Routing and Orchestrator-Workers workflows. RouteLLM paper (arXiv 2406.18665) — a learned router trained on preference data; demonstrates the pattern's headroom, though most production teams still ship rule + classifier + cascade rather than learned routing.

متوسط On 5 August 2026 Meta Superintelligence Labs shipped Muse Code — a terminal coding agent — alongside Muse Spark 1.2, the model co-trained with it. Two products, one release, and the pairing is the interesting part: Meta claims tools that are trained together with the model produce fewer retries and higher-quality output than a generic model steered by a generic harness. Whether or not you buy that claim, the launch is worth reading closely — Muse Code is the closest structural analogue to Claude Code that any competitor has shipped, and a few of its design decisions (the append-only event log, the contributor tier pricing, the three bundled skills) are non-obvious enough to be worth stealing regardless of which agent you actually use day to day. This page is the practical read: what Muse Code actually is, how it compares to Claude Code on the numbers Meta itself published, the pricing trap that shows up on the second read of the pricing table, and where it fits into the AILmanac tour. What you'll learn Understand what Muse Code is architecturally: a terminal agent with a local append-only event log, persistent async background agents, and three shipped skills (/plan, /grill, /goal) Read the Terminal-Bench 2.1 and DeepSWE 1.1 numbers correctly — including the vendor-run caveat that the source review itself flags Know the pricing tiers: $1.25/$4.25 standard vs. $0.10/$0.20 contributor, and what the 12.5×/21.25× discount actually costs you in data terms Get the install command, the platforms supported, and the beta-status caveats before you point this at anything sensitive Place Muse Code next to Claude Code, Codex CLI, and the rest of the coding-agent CLI landscape
documents.s: Muse Code + Muse Spark 1.2: Meta's Terminal Coding Agent

documents.t: Muse Code is a beta terminal coding agent for macOS and Linux, powered by Muse Spark 1.2 — a 1M-token multimodal-input, text-output model — with async background agents, a local append-only event log for crash-safe resume, and three bundled skills (/plan, /grill, /goal); Meta prices the standard tier at $1.25/M input and $4.25/M output, and offers a contributor tier at $0.10/M input and $0.20/M output in exchange for permission to train future Meta models on your prompts and completions.

Muse Code's runtime records every model call, tool run, approval, and edit to a local append-only event log before it executes. Meta describes this as "replay-exact and restart-safe." If the agent crashes mid-task — segfault, laptop lid, expired token, anything — you resume from the log without losing work or having to re-prompt the model to reconstruct state. That's a write-ahead log pattern from database engineering, applied to the harness rather than the storage layer. Two things follow that are worth internalising: Failures during 24-hour runs become recoverable rather than expensive. Meta's own kernel-optimisation case study executed 1,000+ tool calls over 24 hours on NVIDIA Hopper GPUs. Without a durable log, one crash in hour 22 costs the whole run. With one, the model resumes from the last committed event. Post-hoc auditing is trivial. Every decision is on disk, in order, with the tool inputs and outputs. You can inspect what the agent thought, why it called a particular tool, and what came back — without instrumenting anything. The comparable pattern in Claude Code is checkpoints and rewind, which snapshots the workspace so you can step backwards through interactive edits. The Muse Code event log is a different tool for a different problem: rewind lets you undo, while the event log lets the agent resume.
documents.s: 1. The event log is a write-ahead log, and it's what makes long runs safe

documents.t: Two pricing tiers, publicly disclosed: Tier Input ($/M) Cached input ($/M) Output ($/M) You give up Standard $1.25 $0.15 $4.25 Nothing Contributor $0.10 — $0.20 Permission to train future Meta models on your prompts and completions The math on the discount: 12.5× cheaper on input, 21.25× cheaper on output. For a real coding session that reads more than it writes, the effective cost drop lands closer to 15×. The catch is not that Meta will look at your prompts (all frontier vendors log for abuse review by default). The catch is training rights — Meta explicitly retains permission to train future models on your inputs and completions. That means: Anything that would leak trade secrets, PII, licensed code, or a customer's data through a future model output is off-limits. Anything under a share-alike or similar restrictive licence you don't own is off-limits. Anything covered by an NDA is off-limits. Read Meta's exact terms before flipping the toggle — the source reviews are clear that "confirm exact terms and toggle settings in Meta's official docs before running it on anything sensitive." A 12.5× cost reduction on personal side-projects is a genuinely good deal. A 12.5× cost reduction on your employer's monorepo is a legal problem waiting to happen. آخر تحقّق: 2026-08-06. تستشهد هذه الصفحة بحقائق تتغيّر مع الوقت — اعتبر التاريخ أعلاه دليلًا على حداثتها. تأكّد من المصدر الرسمي.

documents.t: Meta published Terminal-Bench 2.1 and DeepSWE 1.1 comparisons that put Muse Spark 1.2 behind Claude Opus 5 on both. That's an unusually honest launch chart, and it's worth reading precisely rather than dismissively. Benchmark Muse Spark 1.2 Claude Opus 5 (paired with Claude Code) Terminal-Bench 2.1 82.9% Higher — Meta ranks it first (external secondhand reporting cites ~86.7%) DeepSWE 1.1 59.3% Higher — Meta ranks it first (score not published in the reviews we could verify) Two caveats before you take those numbers as gospel: Vendor-run methodology. The published numbers are pass@1 averaged over five attempts, each model paired with its own agent product, and Meta itself notes its setup "may not be tuned for third-party models." All numbers are vendor-run, not independent reproductions. Model+harness is the unit of measurement. Terminal-Bench doesn't score a bare model — it scores a model working through an agent. Muse Spark 1.2 is being evaluated inside Muse Code; Opus 5 inside Claude Code. The result is a claim about the pairing, not the model in isolation. Swapping either half changes the number. The practical read: Muse Spark 1.2 is a strong second on the two benchmarks Meta chose to publish, in the harness Meta co-trained it for. That's a defensible position for a v1.2 model against a mature Claude Code / Opus 5 pairing — but "second on the vendor's own chart" is also exactly as strong a claim as it sounds. Don't over-extrapolate.
documents.s: 3. Meta's own charts place Muse Spark 1.2 second, behind Claude Opus 5

documents.t: Muse Code ships three skills out of the box, and the shape of each is instructive: Guided walkthrough1 of 3 1/plan — approval-gated planning⌄ Converts a task into a concrete plan and pauses for human approval before execution. Same pattern as Claude Code's plan mode (docs/claude-code/plan-mode), and the reason is the same: the model is much better at proposing structure than at executing structure it never showed you first. ←PreviousNext→ 2/grill — stress-testing the plan⌄ Runs the plan through adversarial questioning until it stabilises — 'what breaks if X?', 'what did you assume about Y?', 'is there a case where Z fails silently?'. This is the missing step in most naive agent loops: not planning, but pressure-testing the plan before you spend tokens executing it. Nothing about /grill is Meta-specific; you can implement the same discipline with a subagent in any coding CLI. ←PreviousNext→ 3/goal — long-horizon execution⌄ Works toward a specified objective across many tool calls without asking for permission at every step. Pairs with the event log: the human authorises the goal, the log records the trajectory, and the agent runs. The 1,000+ tool call kernel-optimisation case study is a /goal run. ←PreviousNext→ The interesting design pattern here is the plan → grill → goal pipeline: propose, adversarially critique, then execute under a durable log. That decomposition maps cleanly onto workflows you might already be running with Claude Code plan-mode plus subagents — and it's a cleaner mental model than the ad-hoc "keep going until it works" loop most people end up with.
documents.s: 4. The three bundled skills are worth stealing even if you never install Muse Code

documents.t: Availability: macOS and Linux, public beta as of 5 August 2026. No Windows build at launch. Weights are hosted-only — Meta has not published downloadable weights for Muse Spark 1.2. Install Muse Code (macOS / Linux beta) CopyOpen in Claude↗ curl -fsSL https://dev.meta.ai/install.sh | bash Standard security hygiene applies to any curl | bash installer: at minimum, review the script before piping it to a shell. Meta hosts the installer under its own domain, but nothing about the install pattern makes the script inherently safer than any other. Watch out Beta software. Expect breaking changes, undocumented edges, and quota surprises before general availability. Contributor tier trains on your data. Do not flip it on for work code, client code, licensed code, or anything under NDA. Vendor-run benchmarks. Muse Spark 1.2 is second to Claude Opus 5 on Meta's own charts — the numbers to trust are your own on your own repo.

documents.t: Reach for Muse Code when: Your workflow is dominated by long, unattended runs where the event log's crash safety is more valuable than any specific tool integration. The 24-hour kernel-optimisation case study is the shape. You want a second, structurally different opinion on a task. A different model + a different harness is a genuinely different second opinion. The best use of a competitor CLI is often to run the same task through it and compare. You are a solo developer working on side-projects where the contributor tier's data-training trade-off is acceptable, and 12.5×/21.25× cheaper tokens materially change what's affordable. Don't reach for it when: You need MCP tool integration, which is not documented in the launch materials. You need Windows support, which does not exist at launch. You are working on anything covered by an NDA, a restrictive licence, or contains client / employer / PII data, unless you can pay the standard tier and are certain no contributor-tier toggle is on. Your quality bar is "beat Claude Opus 5 on Terminal-Bench 2.1", because on Meta's own numbers it doesn't. Check yourself 0/4 1What does Muse Code's append-only event log actually enable? Streaming responses at higher tokens per secondReplay-exact, restart-safe resume after a crash mid-run, plus post-hoc auditing of every decisionMulti-user collaborative editing of the same terminal sessionAutomatic push to a remote git branch after every tool call 2The contributor tier costs $0.10 / $0.20 per million input/output tokens instead of $1.25 / $4.25. What's the trade? A slower response time and lower rate limitsAccess only to older model checkpoints, not Muse Spark 1.2Permission for Meta to train future models on your prompts and completionsRestriction to non-commercial use only 3Meta's own launch charts place Muse Spark 1.2 where on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and DeepSWE 1.1? First on both, beating Claude Opus 5Second on both, behind Claude Opus 5First on Terminal-Bench, third on DeepSWEThe launch didn't publish comparative benchmarks 4Which of the three bundled skills adversarially stress-tests a plan before execution? /plan — the approval-gated planning skill/grill — asks 'what breaks if X?' and 'what did you assume about Y?' until the plan stabilises/goal — runs toward the objective across many tool callsNone of the bundled skills do this; you have to write your own subagent

documents.t: If you've read coding agent CLIs compared, Muse Code drops in as a new entry with the same shape as Claude Code and Codex CLI — a terminal harness that owns file edits, tool calls, and long-running agent loops. What's different is the runtime discipline (event log) and the tier structure (contributor pricing). If you've read the Opus 5 field guide, the direct point of comparison is that Muse Spark 1.2 is a credible-but-second competitor to Opus 5 on Meta's own numbers, in the harness Meta trained for it. For the broader picture — how to choose across the field — start with choosing a model and what AI costs across providers. If you want to compare techniques rather than products, the plan → grill → goal decomposition is worth composing yourself in Claude Code with subagents and plan mode — you get the discipline without the beta and without the contributor-tier question. آخر تحقّق: 2026-08-06. تستشهد هذه الصفحة بحقائق تتغيّر مع الوقت — اعتبر التاريخ أعلاه دليلًا على حداثتها. تأكّد من المصدر الرسمي.

متقدّم For eighteen months, "multi-agent" meant you wrote the fan-out. You wrote the coordinator prompt, you spawned N calls in parallel, you merged their JSON, you handled the retries. On 9 July 2026 OpenAI collapsed that into a request parameter: multi_agent.enabled: true on the Responses API, wrapped in a consumer feature called Sol Ultra Mode. The model itself decides how many subagents to spawn, runs them in parallel, and synthesises the result — all inside a single HTTP call. No other frontier vendor has shipped a symmetric primitive. This page maps what actually shipped, the numbers behind it, what Anthropic offers instead, and — the part that matters — the three workloads where the native primitive earns its cost and the two where a DIY fan-out still wins. What you'll learn Read the exact Responses API multi-agent request body and know what max_concurrent_subagents actually caps Do the cost math: what 'the model spawns 4 subagents' actually charges you at Sol prices Map the same territory on Anthropic's side — Cowork, Managed Agents, and Claude Code subagents — and see the primitive gap Pick the right primitive per workload: native multi-agent, DIY fan-out, A2A, or a single long turn Avoid the four failure modes that turn a 4-agent Ultra call into a 4x bill with no accuracy win آخر تحقّق: 2026-08-01. The Responses API multi-agent surface is still beta (header OpenAI-Beta: responses_multi_agent=v1). Field names, the default value of max_concurrent_subagents, and which parameters are mutually exclusive with multi-agent mode have all shifted since the 9 July 2026 launch. Re-verify the request shape and the incompatibility list against the linked doc before shipping. تأكّد من المصدر الرسمي.
documents.s: Native Multi-Agent APIs: OpenAI's Responses Multi-Agent Beta vs Building It Yourself

documents.t: Ultra Mode is a consumer skin over multi_agent.enabled: true on the Responses API — a native primitive that lets the model spawn subagents in parallel inside one request, synthesise their outputs, and return a single response. It buys you a small-but-real accuracy bump on parallelisable tasks (Terminal-Bench 2.1: 88.8% → 91.9%), at a token bill that scales roughly linearly with the number of subagents the model chooses to spawn.

Two things landed in the same launch, and it is worth separating them: Ultra Mode — a product toggle inside ChatGPT and Codex. Available on the flagship tier (Sol). When enabled, hard tasks get decomposed into parallel subagent runs before synthesis. Marketed as "spawns 4+ agents"; a few of OpenAI's own GA benchmark charts also show 16-agent configurations on BrowseComp and SEC-Bench Pro, but four is the working default. Responses API multi-agent beta — a developer primitive. The same underlying capability, exposed as multi_agent.enabled: true on client.beta.responses.create(). This is what you'd use to build your own Ultra-like experience. The confusion the marketing left is real: builders keep asking "how do I call Ultra Mode from the API?" The answer is that you don't — you enable the multi-agent beta, which is the primitive under the product feature.

Concretely, this is the shape (Python SDK): Minimal multi-agent Responses API call CopyOpen in Claude↗ from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI() resp = client.beta.responses.create( model="gpt-5.6-sol", input="Audit this repo for auth-bypass patterns and write a report.", multi_agent={ "enabled": True, "max_concurrent_subagents": 3, }, tools=[...], # your MCP tools, function tools, etc. extra_headers={"OpenAI-Beta": "responses_multi_agent=v1"}, ) Four things about this shape are non-obvious: max_concurrent_subagents is not a total budget. It caps active subagent turns across the entire tree at any given moment — root plus descendants. The model can spawn a much larger total number of subagents over the life of the request; it just cannot have more than N running at once. Depth is unbounded. A subagent can itself spawn subagents. There is no fixed cap on tree depth or on total subagent count per run. Your cost surface is not "N calls" — it is a tree the model shapes at runtime. The root synthesises. The root agent is responsible for merging subagent responses into the final answer. You do not get a structured {subagents: [...]} object back; you get one response, and the intermediate agent turns are opaque to your code. Some parameters are silently disabled. reasoning.summary and max_tool_calls are not supported with multi-agent enabled, and the compaction endpoint is unsupported for multi-agent responses. If you rely on reasoning summaries for observability, you lose them the moment you turn this on.

At Sol's GA pricing of $5 input / $30 output per million tokens, the arithmetic is unforgiving. From the builder writeups that reverse-engineered real Ultra runs: A task Ultra decomposes into 2 subagents ≈ 2x the output token cost of a single Sol call — because both subagents generate output, and the root then generates the synthesis on top. A task Ultra spawns 5 subagents for ≈ 5x — same reasoning, plus proportionally more input token replay across the tree. The BrowseComp / SEC-Bench charts that show 16-agent configurations are not free lunch: they are a research-grade demonstration, not a default. At 16 concurrent subagents on Sol, you are looking at a mid-two-digit dollar figure per hard query in output tokens alone. The way to think about it: you are paying for a Monte Carlo of Sol calls plus one synthesis pass on top. Sometimes that buys you enough accuracy to matter. Sometimes it is just a 4x bill for a task a single call would have solved.
documents.s: The cost math nobody prints on the marketing page

documents.t: The published deltas on the parallelisable evals — the workloads Ultra Mode is designed for — are real but modest: Benchmark Sol (single) Sol Ultra Delta What the eval measures Terminal-Bench 2.1 88.8% 91.9% +3.1 Multi-step command-line planning, tool coordination BrowseComp 87.5% 92.2% +4.7 Multi-source web research and synthesis SEC-Bench Pro — 74.3% (single-mode number not published) Regulatory doc reasoning across large corpora Three points about this table: The +3–5 point band is consistent with what parallel sampling has historically bought you on other frontiers (best-of-N, self-consistency). The primitive is genuinely useful; the delta is not a step-change. These are the best case — evaluations chosen to showcase the mode. On sequential tasks (a linear code edit, a single file rewrite, a short chat), Ultra adds synthesis latency and cost without moving accuracy. On the same Terminal-Bench 2.1 chart, Anthropic's Opus 4.8 scored 78.9% — meaning Sol Ultra's lead comes from both the better base model and the multi-agent boost stacked on top. If you migrate to Sol Ultra from Opus, do not attribute the whole gap to the multi-agent primitive.

Anthropic has not shipped a symmetric API primitive. The closest analogues each solve a different slice of the same problem: Cowork — a product surface. An agentic desktop workspace where an agent does sustained multi-step work alongside the user. Comparable to Ultra Mode as a feature, but not as an API primitive. Managed Agents and managed-agents memory stores — a hosted agent loop with persistent state and scheduling. Fills the "long-running background agent" slot, not the "spawn 4 in parallel and merge" slot. Claude Code subagents and the subagent fleet limits — a first-class subagent primitive, but scoped to the Claude Code CLI. Documented, spawnable in parallel, and the closest analogue to multi_agent.enabled — with the important difference that you write the coordinator prompt yourself. Building Agents on the Messages API — the DIY path. You fan out N messages.create calls in parallel, you write the synthesis prompt, you handle retries. Same result, more code. The gap: no Anthropic API surface currently lets you flip a single boolean and have the model itself decide how many subagents to spawn and merge their work. If you want that behavior against Claude, you build it — see Cowork & Agent Teams for the product-side story and Managed Agents for the hosted-loop primitive.

Guided walkthrough1 of 5 1Is the task genuinely parallelisable?⌄ If subtasks can run without waiting on each other's results — audit a repo, research a topic across many sources, refactor N files independently — a fan-out shape earns its cost. If the task is sequential (edit A, then read A's result, then edit B), any multi-agent primitive adds synthesis overhead for no gain. ←PreviousNext→ 2Do you need to inspect intermediate turns?⌄ Native multi-agent (Ultra, Responses multi-agent beta) hides subagent turns from your code. If you need audit trails, per-subagent cost attribution, or the ability to inject mid-run — build the fan-out yourself. Claude Code's subagents give you visibility; the Responses API multi-agent beta does not. ←PreviousNext→ 3Are the subagents crossing a trust boundary?⌄ If subtasks belong to different orgs, clouds, or vendors, you are outside the scope of any single-vendor primitive. Use A2A — see /docs/models/a2a-protocol-agent-to-agent. Native multi-agent is intra-model; A2A is inter-agent. ←PreviousNext→ 4Is cost bounded or open-ended?⌄ Native multi-agent trees are runtime-shaped: you cannot predict the token bill from the request. If your app has a per-request cost SLA, prefer DIY fan-out where you control the fan-out width — or set a hard max_output_tokens ceiling on the root. ←PreviousNext→ 5Do you need the +3–5 accuracy points?⌄ If your eval says the task is 85%-solvable with a single call and 90% is the difference between shipping and not, native multi-agent is a low-friction way to buy it. If a single Sol or Opus call already solves the task, Ultra is a 4x bill for a 0-point gain. ←PreviousNext→
documents.s: Picking the right primitive per workload

documents.t: Turning it on for sequential tasks. The model still decomposes and synthesises even when the task doesn't parallelise. You pay for coordination overhead on work that never needed it. Rule of thumb: if you can't articulate what the second subagent would be doing while the first runs, don't enable multi-agent. Leaving reasoning-summary observability on your dashboard. reasoning.summary is silently unsupported with multi-agent. If your monitoring depends on it, you'll get empty fields and think the model isn't thinking. Ship a schema change before you flip the flag. Using max_tool_calls as a safety limit. Also silently disabled with multi-agent. The safety story you thought you had — "at most 20 tool calls per request" — is gone. Enforce tool-call ceilings at the tool-adapter layer, not via the request parameter. Assuming max_concurrent_subagents is a cost cap. It caps active subagents at a moment, not total spawned over the request. A single Ultra call can spawn dozens of subagents sequentially and still respect a max_concurrent_subagents: 3 limit. If cost is your ceiling, add a request-level max_output_tokens.
documents.s: Four failure modes that turn Ultra into a 4x bill for nothing

documents.t: Two adjacent primitives are often confused with it: Not n > 1 sampling. OpenAI's older n parameter samples multiple completions and returns all of them; you pick one. Multi-agent runs different subagents doing different work and synthesises their outputs. The former is temperature-sampling; the latter is task decomposition. Not batch inference. The batch API processes many independent requests in the background. Multi-agent is many coordinated subagents inside one interactive request. Batch is throughput-oriented, multi-agent is result-oriented.

The A2A protocol (see A2A: The Agent-to-Agent Protocol) covers inter-vendor multi-agent. multi_agent.enabled: true covers intra-model multi-agent. The unfilled slot is a cross-vendor primitive — the model on vendor A spawns a subagent on vendor B and merges the result — and there is no public spec for it yet. When it lands, it will land as A2A + a native handoff verb, not as a new API on either side. Watch that space. Check yourself 0/4 1What does max_concurrent_subagents cap on the Responses multi-agent beta? The total number of subagents the request can ever spawnThe number of active subagent turns at any moment across the whole tree, excluding the rootThe tree depth (how deeply subagents can spawn their own subagents)The number of tool calls each subagent can make 2You enable multi-agent and your monitoring dashboard suddenly shows empty reasoning-summary fields. What happened? The model failed silently — retry the requestreasoning.summary is unsupported when multi_agent is enabled; the API silently drops itThe subagents ran but the synthesis pass timed outYour beta header is wrong 3You need parallel subagents that run in different customer accounts across two vendors. Which primitive is correct? OpenAI Responses API multi-agent beta with max_concurrent_subagents: 2Claude Code subagentsThe A2A protocol, with each vendor exposing an Agent CardGPT-5.6 Ultra Mode via ChatGPT 4Which of these is a poor candidate for Ultra Mode / multi_agent.enabled? Auditing a large codebase for a class of vulnerability across many filesMulti-source web research where each source can be read independentlyA single-file code rewrite where each edit depends on the previous oneComparing regulatory filings across many companies لا توجد بطاقات بعد — أضف بعضها لبدء المذاكرة. 🃏

What you'll learn Explain what open-code-review does differently from asking Claude Code or Codex to "review my PR": which steps are code, which are model Read its benchmark honestly — the 4.7x precision headline, the 20% recall ceiling, and why a newer Claude model scored lower Run a first review with any provider (Claude, GPT, Gemini, Qwen, DeepSeek, a local Ollama model) and preview the file filter without spending a token Choose between OCR-managed reviews and delegation mode, where your Claude Code or Codex subscription does the thinking Wire it into CI without walking into the pull_request_target and false-positive traps Every team that turned on coding agents in 2026 hit the same wall: the code arrives faster than anyone can read it. "Just ask the agent to review it too" is the obvious answer, and it mostly produces a wall of comments nobody trusts. open-code-review (the ocr CLI) is Alibaba's answer, open-sourced on May 18, 2026 after roughly two years inside the company, and it is back on GitHub Trending this week with 27.5k stars and a release on September 15. It is worth a page because its core idea transfers to anything you build with Claude, GPT or an open model: take the steps that must not go wrong away from the model, and hand the model only the judgement calls.
documents.s: Open Code Review: Alibaba's Hybrid AI Reviewer vs Claude Code, Codex and Any Model (2026)

documents.t: The maintainers name three failure modes they saw when general-purpose agents review code with a skill or prompt, and they map almost one-to-one to what Claude Code users complain about: Failure in a pure-agent review What OCR does in code instead Incomplete coverage — on big diffs the agent quietly reviews some files and skips others A deterministic five-gate file filter decides exactly which files are reviewed, and each one is dispatched; the model cannot "forget" a file Position drift — the comment points at the wrong line or file A separate positioning module anchors each comment by matching the code snippet the model quotes against the diff, then the whole file, and only then asks the model to relocate it Unstable quality — small prompt changes swing the result Rules are matched to files by glob patterns, not chosen by the model; related files (for example message_en.properties and message_zh.properties) are bundled and each bundle runs as an isolated sub-agent The model keeps the parts it is actually good at: deciding what to look at next and pulling in context. It gets a small, purpose-built toolset — read a file range, read another file's diff, grep the repo, find a file by name, emit a comment, finish — which the team says they distilled from tool-call traces in production. A final reflection/filter pass throws out weak comments before you see them. Guided walkthrough1 of 5 11. Build the diff⌄ Workspace (staged, unstaged and untracked), a branch range computed from the merge-base, a single commit, or `ocr scan` for whole files with no diff. Git 2.41+ is required. ←PreviousNext→ 22. Filter files in code⌄ Five gates in order: binary, your exclude list (always wins), your include list (bypasses the rest), extension allowlist, built-in test-file patterns. `vendor/`, `node_modules/` and similar are dropped before the gates and can never be included. ←PreviousNext→ 33. Match rules and bundle⌄ Each file gets its rule from a priority chain (CLI `--rule`, then project `.opencodereview/rule.json`, then your user file, then the built-in rules). Related files are grouped; groups run in parallel, 8 at a time by default. ←PreviousNext→ 44. Plan, then review in rounds⌄ A read-only plan call runs only for big changes (one file with 50+ changed lines, or 2+ files totalling 100+). Then the main tool loop runs 1, 2 or 3 rounds depending on `--effort`; later rounds see earlier findings and skip the plan, which the docs say otherwise acts as a coverage ceiling. ←PreviousNext→ 55. Anchor, filter, output⌄ Comments are anchored to lines, weak ones are filtered, and results go to text, JSON or SARIF — or back to your PR through a CI recipe. ←PreviousNext→
documents.s: The idea: code for the rails, a model for the judgement

documents.t: Alibaba publishes results on AACR-Bench, its own dataset on Hugging Face: 50 open-source repositories, 200 real pull requests, 10 languages, and 1,505 issues annotated and cross-checked by 80+ senior engineers. Selected rows from the leaderboard in the README: Reviewer Model F1 Precision Recall Tokens / review Time OCR v1.3.1 Claude Opus 4.6 25.1% 33.9% (301 of 889) 20.0% 385K 1m23s OCR v1.8.7 Qwen3.8-Max 23.0% 33.9% 17.4% 334K 5m14s OCR v1.3.1 GPT-5.5 21.0% 32.1% 15.5% 422K 2m51s OCR v1.3.1 Claude Opus 4.8 17.9% 37.8% 11.7% 352K 1m06s Claude Code v2.1.169 Claude Opus 4.8 14.1% 15.9% 12.7% 2,062K 5m38s Claude Code v2.1.169 Claude Opus 4.6 11.6% 7.2% (435 of 5,980) 28.9% 5,664K 13m06s Codex v0.140.0 GPT-5.5 8.4% 27.8% 4.9% 525K 2m58s Three things in that table are more interesting than the headline. 1. The precision gap is really a comment-volume gap. With Opus 4.6, Claude Code posted 5,980 comments across 200 PRs — about 30 per PR — and 7% of them matched a real annotated issue. OCR posted 889 (about 4.4 per PR) and 34% matched. Claude Code actually found more real issues (435 vs 301, the higher recall). The difference is noise, and noise is what gets an AI reviewer switched off: one Hacker News commenter put it as "if 7/8 flagged items are fine, people will ignore warnings." 2. The best reviewer on the board finds one real issue in five. The top recall anywhere is Claude Code's 28.9%, and OCR's best is 20%. Even allowing for a strict, opinionated ground truth (a point raised on HN), no configuration here is a merge gate. Treat any AI reviewer as a filter that catches some bugs cheaply, not as the thing that says a PR is safe. That fits a wider pattern AILmanac covers in the verification bottleneck. 3. A newer model scored lower, and the headline ratios shrink with it. Inside OCR, Opus 4.8 had the best precision on the board (37.8%) but lower recall (11.7%) than Opus 4.6, so its F1 dropped from 25.1% to 17.9%. Stronger models were more conservative — the same thing an HN tester reported with GPT-5.x. Against Claude Code on Opus 4.8, OCR's edge is about 2.4x precision and about 6x fewer tokens, not the 4.7x and ~1/15 you get from the Opus 4.6 rows (the README rounds its overall claim to "~1/9"). And the Claude Code and Codex rows are several versions old. Also keep in mind that this is the vendor's benchmark, built by the team that builds the tool. An early independent test on HN (10 PRs from a different benchmark) measured roughly 12% precision; the maintainers traced it to a broken tool call and said it was fixed. Run it on your own recent PRs before you believe any row.

ocr is a Go binary shipped through npm. It speaks the Anthropic, OpenAI Chat Completions, OpenAI Responses and Bedrock protocols, and ships presets for Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, DeepSeek, Kimi, Z.ai, MiniMax, xAI, DashScope (Qwen) and more; anything else is a custom provider with a URL and a protocol. Install, configure, and dry-run the filter CopyOpen in Claude↗ npm install -g @alibaba-group/open-code-review # Interactive: pick a provider, paste a key, pick a model; it runs a connectivity test ocr config provider ocr config model ocr llm test cd your-repo # See exactly which files would be reviewed, and why others are excluded — no LLM call ocr review --preview # Review your branch against main, with context the model can't infer ocr review --from main --to my-branch --background "Adds rate limiting to the public API" Things the docs spell out that save you an afternoon: Already using Claude Code? If no config file or OCR_LLM_* variables are set, ocr falls back to ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL, ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN and ANTHROPIC_MODEL. It takes the first complete URL-token-model triple it finds, so a stale config file silently beats your environment variables. Local models need native tool calling. OCR drives the whole review through tool calls. A model that only writes tool calls as text (the FAQ names deepseek-r1) loops on "No tool calls parsed" and returns zero comments. Pick an Ollama model tagged for tools, such as qwen3; see running models locally. --effort is the quality/cost dial. low is 1 review round, medium (default) 2, high 3; the per-group timeout scales with it. --max-tokens-budget puts a hard cap on total tokens and still publishes partial results. --background matters. The CLI reference calls it one of the highest-leverage flags: the model only sees the diff and what it chooses to read, not your ticket. A comment at start_line: 0 is real but couldn't be anchored — usually the model paraphrased the code instead of quoting it, or the diff has CRLF or mixed indentation.
